slides.title: Democratic Values in Panchayati Raj
slides.storyContext: Ravi reflects on what he's learned: village democracy is messy, slow, and sometimes corrupt—but it gives ordinary people power.

points.label: Decentralization
points.text: Power is spread to villages, not concentrated in capitals. Villagers decide their own fate.

points.label: Accountability
points.text: Leaders face villagers in meetings. Poor decisions or corruption are exposed quickly.

points.label: Participation
points.text: Everyone can speak in meetings and vote. No one is locked out of decision-making.

points.label: Inclusivity
points.text: Reserved seats ensure women, SCs, and STs are heard. Minorities can't be ignored.

slides.inSimpleWords: Panchayati Raj values: locals decide, leaders are accountable, everyone participates, and minorities are included.

slides.title: Example: A Sarpanch's Accountability
slides.storyContext: After 5 years, Lakshmi's mother's term ends. The villagers evaluate: roads were fixed, water improved, but school remains unfinished. A new candidate challenges her with a clearer education plan.

example.problem: A Sarpanch completed 2 of 4 promised projects. Should voters re-elect her or choose someone new?
example.solution: Voters must decide. Democracy means evaluating performance. A 50% completion rate might be acceptable if funds were limited, or it might indicate poor planning. This teaches accountability and informed voting.

slides.inSimpleWords: Voters can judge a leader's performance and choose to replace them if dissatisfied. This is democratic accountability.

slides.title: Role of Block and District Panchayats
slides.storyContext: Ravi learns how the three-tier system works in practice. If his village Panchayat needs resources beyond its budget, it escalates to the Block Panchayat, which coordinates resources across 40-50 villages.

points.label: Block Panchayat
points.text: Covers 40-50 villages. Coordinates development programs, supervises village Panchayats, and distributes funds from state to village level.

points.label: District Panchayat
points.text: Covers an entire district (100+ villages/blocks). Plans large projects (highways, major irrigation), manages district-level schemes.

points.label: Coordination
points.text: The three tiers work together. A village identifies need, Block supports, District resources are tapped. Power flows both ways.

slides.inSimpleWords: Block and District Panchayats coordinate resources and support village Panchayats. Together, the three tiers form a complete democratic system.

slides.title: The Village Rules
slides.storyContext: Ravi has learned that Panchayati Raj is democracy at its most authentic form. The villagers are not distant from power—they ARE the power.

points.text: Panchayati Raj means villages govern themselves through elected councils.
Three tiers: Village Panchayat, Block Panchayat, District Panchayat.
The Panchayat handles water, roads, schools, health, and local disputes.
Women and SC/ST members have reserved seats to ensure equal voice.
Villages get funds from local taxes and state/national grants.
The Panchayat budget is public—anyone can check how money is spent.

slides.inSimpleWords: In Panchayati Raj, villagers are in charge. They elect leaders and decide what their village needs.

subject: Social Science
title: The City Runs: Urban Local Bodies
hook: How do cities govern themselves? Who fixes roads, collects garbage, and runs schools in a city?

characters.name: Isha
characters.role: A 12-year-old from a mid-sized city in Karnataka

characters.name: Isha's mother
characters.role: A city employee working in the municipal corporation

characters.name: Councillor Deepak
characters.role: An elected ward councillor in the city

slides.title: Grassroots Democracy - Urban Local Government
slides.storyContext: Isha lives in a city of 2 million people. Every morning, she sees garbage collectors, sweepers, and water tankers on the streets. She wonders: 'Who employs them? Who decides if a road gets fixed or a new park is built?' Her mother says: 'The Municipal Corporation (Nagar Nigam). It's the city's government.'

slides.title: The Ward Meeting
slides.storyContext: Isha attends a public meeting in her ward (neighborhood). Councillor Deepak asks residents: 'What are the top 3 problems in our ward?' People complain: 'The water supply fails twice a week.' 'Potholes on our street.' 'The street light outside the school is broken.' Deepak takes notes and says: 'I'll take these to the Municipal Corporation's budget meeting next month.' Isha sees: even in a big city, local democracy is real.

slides.title: Behind the Scenes: A Garbage Collector's Morning
slides.storyContext: Isha's mother shows her a garbage collection route. The city is divided into zones, each with a supervisor. Garbage trucks start at 5 AM. Sweepers walk every street. Isha learns: cities need thousands of workers to stay clean.

slides.title: Types of Urban Local Bodies (Municipalities)
slides.storyContext: Isha learns that India's cities are governed by three types of municipal bodies, depending on size and importance.

points.label: Nagar Nigam (Municipal Corporation)
points.text: For large cities (population above 10 lakhs). Examples: Mumbai, Delhi, Bangalore. Headed by a Mayor and has a large elected council.

points.label: Nagar Palika (Municipality)
points.text: For medium cities (1-10 lakhs population). Examples: Nagpur, Jaipur. Headed by a President/Mayor and a smaller council.

points.label: Nagar Panchayat (Town Council)
points.text: For small towns and growing areas. Headed by a Chairperson and has a small council. Transitional between village and city governance.

example.problem: Isha's city has 2 million people. Should it be governed by a Nagar Panchayat, Nagar Palika, or Nagar Nigam?
example.solution: A Nagar Nigam (Municipal Corporation) is best for such a large city. It has the most resources and departments to handle 2 million people's needs.

slides.inSimpleWords: Big cities have a Nagar Nigam, medium cities have a Nagar Palika, and small towns have a Nagar Panchayat. Each type is suited to different city sizes.

slides.title: Example: Why City Size Determines Governance Type
slides.storyContext: Isha compares three cities: City A (2 million, Bangalore), City B (500,000, Nagpur), City C (50,000, small town).

example.problem: Which city needs Nagar Nigam, which needs Nagar Palika, and which needs Nagar Panchayat?
example.solution: A→Nigam (2M requires 60+ councillors, multiple departments). B→Palika (500K requires 30-40 councillors). C→Panchayat (50K requires 10-15 members). Governance scales with size.

slides.inSimpleWords: Larger cities need bigger governments with more departments and resources.

slides.title: Structure of a Municipal Corporation
slides.storyContext: Isha's mother works in the Municipal Corporation. She shows Isha the organization: a Mayor (elected leader), Councillors (elected representatives from wards), a Municipal Commissioner (top bureaucrat), and various departments.

points.label: Mayor (elected)
points.text: The elected head of the corporation. Symbolic role (like the President) + presides over council meetings. Elected by voters or by councillors.

points.label: Deputy Mayor (elected)
points.text: Assists the Mayor. Often from a specific community or gender to ensure representation.

points.label: Councillors (elected)
points.text: Elected from wards (subdivisions of the city). Each ward (30,000-50,000 people) elects 1-2 councillors. They represent ward interests in the council.

points.label: Municipal Commissioner (appointed bureaucrat)
points.text: The top official, NOT elected. Responsible for day-to-day operations: hiring staff, collecting taxes, awarding contracts.

example.problem: Isha's ward councillor promises to fix all roads. But the Mayor says only 50% can be repaired. Who has power?
example.solution: The Mayor and Commissioner have more power. The councillor represents the ward, but the corporation's budget and resources are managed by the Mayor and Commissioner. The councillor must convince them in council meetings.

slides.inSimpleWords: A city has elected leaders (Mayor, Councillors) and a top bureaucrat (Commissioner). Elected leaders make policy; the Commissioner runs day-to-day operations.

slides.title: The Mayor's Public Meeting
slides.storyContext: The new Mayor holds a town hall. Citizens ask: 'Why are potholes not fixed?' 'Where is the metro funding?' 'When will we get 24-hour water?' The Mayor listens (mostly), takes some notes, and promises action. Isha sees: mayors must face public pressure.

slides.title: Functions of Urban Local Bodies: The Services They Provide
slides.storyContext: Isha's mother lists what the corporation does: water supply, garbage collection, sewerage, roads, street lights, property registration, building permits, and vaccination camps.

points.label: Water and sanitation
points.text: Supplying drinking water, managing sewerage systems, drains, and ensuring public toilets.

points.label: Solid waste management
points.text: Collecting garbage, street cleaning, composting, and landfill management.

points.label: Public health
points.text: Running vaccination camps, health clinics, maternity centers, and disease control programs.

points.label: Roads and transport
points.text: Building and maintaining roads, street lights, public buses, parking, and traffic management.

points.label: Planning and permits
points.text: Granting building permits, planning new residential areas, ensuring city beautification.

points.label: Social welfare
points.text: Running schools, community centers, public libraries, markets, and welfare programs for the poor.

example.problem: During monsoon, Isha's street floods with sewage. Who should fix it?
example.solution: The Municipal Corporation (sewerage and drainage department). If they delay, Isha's ward councillor can raise it in the council or approach the Commissioner. The corporation is accountable to residents.

slides.inSimpleWords: The city's municipal body provides water, removes garbage, repairs roads, runs hospitals, and maintains everything that makes city life possible.

slides.title: Example: A Day in the Garbage Department
slides.storyContext: Isha's mother shows her the garbage collection system. The city produces 500 tons of garbage daily. The corporation must collect, transport, and dispose of it.

example.problem: If 1 garbage truck collects from 50 houses, the city has 2 million people (400,000 homes). How many trucks does it need?
example.solution: 400,000 homes ÷ 50 = 8,000 trucks needed. But trucks run multiple routes (3-4 per day). So maybe 2,000-2,500 trucks. The corporation also needs dumping sites, and now, recycling centers. Managing garbage is complex and expensive.

slides.inSimpleWords: Cities need thousands of workers and vehicles to stay clean. Waste management is invisible but essential.

slides.title: Ward System and Representation
slides.storyContext: Isha's city is divided into 100 wards. Her ward (Ward 45) has about 40,000 people. Every 5 years, they elect 2 councillors—1 from a general seat and 1 from a reserved seat (women, SC, or ST).

points.label: Ward definition
points.text: A city is divided into wards (geographic subdivisions). Each ward elects 1-2 councillors who represent its interests.

points.label: Representation formula
points.text: Usually: 1 councillor per 30,000-50,000 people. A city of 2 million might have 40-50 wards.

points.label: Reserved seats
points.text: Like Panchayats, municipal wards have reserved seats for women (1/3 of all seats), SCs, and STs (proportional to population).

points.label: Councillor's role
points.text: Represent the ward in council, bring grievances, vote on city budget, and advocate for local projects.

example.problem: Ward 45 has 40,000 people but elects 2 councillors. How do they represent everyone?
example.solution: The 2 councillors meet with residents regularly, listen to complaints, and raise them in the city council. They also hold public meetings (like Panchayat meetings) to discuss ward problems.

slides.inSimpleWords: A city is divided into wards. Each ward elects councillors to represent their interests in the city council.

slides.title: The Pothole Problem
slides.storyContext: Councillor Deepak's ward has 200 potholes. He asks the corporation's roads department: 'When will they be fixed?' The answer: 'In 3 months, if budget permits.' He negotiates and gets them on the priority list. Isha learns: councillors must push and negotiate.

slides.title: Finance: How Cities Earn and Spend Money
slides.storyContext: Isha's mother explains: 'The city needs money for water pipes, garbage trucks, salaries. Where does it come from?'

points.label: Property tax
points.text: Charged on every building in the city (4-10% of property value annually). Largest source of city revenue.

points.label: Water and sewerage charges
points.text: Residents pay for water and sewerage. Commerces pay more for large consumption.

points.label: Market and parking fees
points.text: Vendors in city markets pay rent; vehicles pay parking fees.

points.label: State and national grants
points.text: State government provides grants; national schemes like AMRUT (water and sanitation) provide central funding.

points.label: Budget transparency
points.text: The city budget is published. The council debates and approves it. Anyone can demand an audit.

example.problem: Isha's property tax is 5,000 rupees/year. The city collects 50 crores from 1 million properties. But the budget shows 200 crores needed (water supply costs 80 crores, garbage costs 30 crores, salaries 60 crores, roads 30 crores). Where does the extra money come from?
example.solution: Water and sewerage charges (30 crores), market fees (20 crores), state grants (40 crores), and borrowing/bonds. The city must plan carefully.

slides.inSimpleWords: Cities earn money from property tax, water charges, market fees, and government grants. The budget must balance income and spending.

slides.title: Example: Municipal Revenue Sources
slides.storyContext: Isha's city budget for the year is 300 crores. Let's trace where it comes from.

example.problem: A city of 2 million (1 million properties) needs 300 crores. Property tax (4% avg): 40 crores. Water charges: 30 crores. Parking/market fees: 20 crores. That's only 90 crores. Where does the rest come from?
example.solution: State grant (120 crores), central scheme funds (60 crores), and borrowing/bonds (30 crores). Total = 300 crores. Cities depend heavily on grants and borrowed money, not just local taxes.

slides.inSimpleWords: Most city budgets rely on a mix of local taxes, government grants, and borrowing.

slides.title: A Water Pipe Breaks Under the Street
slides.storyContext: One morning, a main water pipe bursts under Isha's street. For 2 days, her neighborhood has no water. The corporation's repair team arrives, digs, replaces the pipe, and tests. Isha watches and wonders: 'How many problems like this happen every day?'

slides.title: The Mayor's Tough Decision
slides.storyContext: The city's budget is tight. The Mayor must choose: (1) Upgrade aging water pipes (critical but expensive: 100 crores), (2) Build new parks (popular but not urgent: 50 crores), or (3) Fix potholes and improve drainage (immediate need: 80 crores). She chooses (1) and (3), deferring parks. Isha learns: leadership means making unpopular choices for long-term benefit.

slides.title: Urban Democracy: How Cities Listen to Citizens
slides.storyContext: Isha learns that cities have systems for citizen participation: ward meetings, public hearings on big projects, and grievance committees.

points.label: Ward meetings
points.text: Monthly or quarterly meetings where councillors listen to residents' problems and complaints.

points.label: Public hearings
points.text: Before major projects (building a new road, highway, hospital), the corporation holds hearings where citizens can object or suggest changes.

points.label: Grievance cells
points.text: Citizens can lodge complaints through online portals or offices. The corporation must respond within a set time.

points.label: Right to Information (RTI)
points.text: Citizens can demand documents showing how the corporation spent money or made decisions. Transparency prevents corruption.

slides.inSimpleWords: Cities have systems to listen to citizens: ward meetings, public hearings, grievance cells, and information rights.

slides.title: A Citizen's Complaint Works
slides.storyContext: Isha's neighbor files a complaint about a broken water line through the corporation's mobile app. He attaches photos and a date. Within 2 weeks, the corporation responds, schedules a repair, and completes it. He files a follow-up through RTI asking for details. Isha sees: citizens can hold the corporation accountable through systems.

slides.title: Challenges Facing Urban Local Bodies
slides.storyContext: Cities face real challenges: rapid growth, aging infrastructure, slums, overcrowding, and budget shortfalls that make it hard to provide services to everyone.

points.label: Infrastructure deficit
points.text: Old pipes leak water, roads have potholes, and sewers overflow. Upgrading costs billions.

points.label: Rapid urbanization
points.text: People move to cities faster than infrastructure can be built. Slums grow because formal housing is expensive.

points.label: Budget constraints
points.text: Cities need more money but rely on grants and debt. Property tax collection is low (many properties unregistered or exempt).

points.label: Service delivery gaps
points.text: Water, waste, and health services don't reach everyone equally. Poor neighborhoods are often neglected.

slides.inSimpleWords: Cities face real challenges: aging infrastructure, rapid growth, slums, and budget shortfalls that make providing services difficult.

slides.title: Challenge: A Councillor's Dilemma
slides.storyContext: Councillor Deepak has a limited fund (2 crores) for his ward this year. He has 5 urgent demands from residents: (1) Fix 10 km of broken roads (1.5 crores), (2) Install 50 new street lights (50 lakhs), (3) Build a community health center (1 crore), (4) Improve the school building (75 lakhs), (5) Repair the old park (50 lakhs). Total: 3.75 crores. He can only choose 2-3. What should he prioritize?

example.problem: Which 2-3 projects should Councillor Deepak fund from 2 crores?
example.solution: One answer: (1) Road repairs (1.5 crores—affects traffic and commerce), (2) Street lights (50 lakhs—safety issue). Defer health center and school. Another answer: (3) Health center (1 crore—critical for poor) + (2) Street lights (50 lakhs) + small portions of roads. Justify your choice based on urgency and impact. This teaches real governance trade-offs.

slides.inSimpleWords: A city councillor must choose which projects to fund. Like the Panchayat, there's limited money and unlimited needs. Choices reflect values.

slides.title: Challenge: Handling a Water Crisis
slides.storyContext: During a dry summer, the city's water reserves drop to 10%. Residents get water only 2 hours a day. The corporation must decide: ration water or build a new pipeline (costs 50 crores, takes 2 years)?

example.problem: Water shortage: (a) Strict rationing (1 hour per day per household) or (b) borrow money and build new pipeline?
example.solution: Both. Immediate rationing prevents collapse. Long-term investment in new water sources (pipeline, treatment plant, recycling). A real crisis teaches hard choices about sustainability and planning.

slides.inSimpleWords: Cities face resource crises. Leaders must balance short-term survival with long-term planning.

slides.title: Election Day: Isha Grows Up
slides.storyContext: Years later, Isha is an adult. She votes for the new ward councillor. The incumbent (who fixed potholes but ignored slums) loses to a challenger who promises slum upgrades. Isha sees: democracy means power can change hands.

slides.title: Example: How a Ward Councillor Advocates
slides.storyContext: Councillor Deepak identifies 5 key issues in his ward from public meetings. He prioritizes them, attaches data and photos, and presents to the council with a budget proposal.

example.problem: Ward issues: (1) 100 potholes (5 lakhs), (2) No streetlights (3 lakhs), (3) Water pollution (7 lakhs). Total: 15 lakhs. Deepak can push only 2. Which?
example.solution: Health first: pollution (7L) affects everyone. Safety second: streetlights (3L). Defer potholes. Total: 10L. A good councillor explains trade-offs to residents and rallies support.

slides.inSimpleWords: Councillors must advocate for their wards by presenting needs with data and negotiating with the corporation.

slides.title: Comparing Rural and Urban Local Governance
slides.storyContext: Isha visits her village cousin Ravi. She notices: villages have Panchayats, cities have Nagar Nigams. Both are democratic, but operate differently due to size and complexity.

points.label: Panchayat (rural)
points.text: Small, direct democracy. Meetings in open spaces, everyone attends, decisions by consensus or simple vote. Personal and quick.

points.label: Nagar Nigam (urban)
points.text: Large, representative democracy. Too many people for direct participation, so residents elect councillors who vote. Formal and structured.

points.label: Similarities
points.text: Both have elected leaders, budgets, public funds, and accountability. Both aim to serve residents' needs.

points.label: Challenges differ
points.text: Villages struggle with funds; cities struggle with demand and corruption. Both need citizen participation to work.

slides.inSimpleWords: Rural and urban local governance are different systems suited to different contexts, but both are forms of grassroots democracy.

slides.title: Urban Evolution: From Crisis to Progress
slides.storyContext: Isha's city faced water crisis 10 years ago. Through coordination of multiple Palika, state funding, and citizen pressure, a new water treatment plant was built. Now, water is reliable. Isha sees: urban local bodies can deliver if well-run.

slides.title: Election Night: A New Councillor
slides.storyContext: Isha votes for the first time. Her favourite candidate (a young woman from the ward) wins. The new councillor promises monthly ward meetings and an online complaint system. Isha feels: her vote mattered, and things will improve.

slides.title: The City Runs
slides.storyContext: Isha now realizes: cities are complex, but they're still democratic. Elected councillors, transparent budgets, and public meetings ensure residents have a voice.

points.text: Three types of urban local bodies: Nagar Nigam (big cities), Nagar Palika (medium cities), Nagar Panchayat (towns).
Cities are divided into wards. Each ward elects councillors to represent residents.
A Mayor heads the corporation; a Commissioner handles day-to-day operations.
Urban bodies provide water, garbage collection, roads, health, and social services.
Cities earn money from property tax, water charges, market fees, and government grants.
Urban local democracy ensures residents have a voice in city decisions.

slides.inSimpleWords: Cities are governed by elected councillors and professional administrators. Together, they provide water, roads, health, and safety to millions of residents.

subject: Social Science
title: Work Feeds the World: Understanding Labor
hook: Why does work matter? What does a farmer, a teacher, or a builder contribute to society?

characters.name: Mohan
characters.role: A 12-year-old from a farming family in Punjab

characters.name: Priya
characters.role: His friend whose father is a doctor

characters.name: Grandmother Savitri
characters.role: A retired schoolteacher who now does community work

slides.title: The Value of Work
slides.storyContext: Mohan watches his father wake at dawn to work in the fields. Priya's father works long hours in a hospital. Grandmother Savitri, retired from teaching, now volunteers in the village school. Mohan wonders: 'Why do people work? Is farming less important than being a doctor? Is volunteer work real work?'

slides.title: Where Does Your Food Come From?
slides.storyContext: Grandmother Savitri asks the children: 'Close your eyes. Imagine a day without food, without clothes, without a house, without schools, hospitals, or roads. Who made all this?' 'Farmers grow food,' says Mohan. 'Tailors make clothes,' says Priya. 'Builders construct houses,' adds Mohan. 'And teachers educate children,' finishes Savitri. Every piece of the world is built by someone's labor. Every job matters.

image.alt: Where Does Your Food Come From? — The Value of Work

slides.title: Mohan's Father: A Day in the Fields
slides.storyContext: Mohan joins his father at 4 AM. They walk to the wheat field. For 12 hours, his father plows, sows, waters, and repairs equipment. By evening, he's exhausted but satisfied. 'This work feeds our family and the nation,' he tells Mohan. Mohan realizes: hard work deserves respect.

slides.title: What is Work? Paid and Unpaid Work
slides.storyContext: Grandmother Savitri teaches: 'Work is not just jobs that pay money. Work is any effort that produces something useful.'

points.label: Paid work (employment)
points.text: Work done for wages: farming, teaching, driving, nursing, engineering, shopkeeping. The person receives money in exchange.

points.label: Unpaid work
points.text: Work done without direct payment: cooking at home, caring for children, washing clothes, gardening for family, community volunteer work.

points.label: Why unpaid work matters
points.text: Families survive on unpaid work. Women do most unpaid work globally. Without it, society collapses.

points.label: Work has dignity
points.text: No job is shameful. A cleaner's work is as valuable as a CEO's work. Both contribute to society.

example.problem: Mohan's mother cooks for the family daily (5 hours) but earns no money. Is she working?
example.solution: Yes, absolutely. She's doing crucial unpaid work. If this work were paid, a family would spend 15,000+ rupees monthly on a cook. Her unpaid labor saves the family and sustains it. Unpaid work is still work.

slides.inSimpleWords: Work includes both paid jobs and unpaid household tasks. Both are valuable. Cooking, childcare, and housework are real work.

slides.title: Priya's Mother: A Day in the House
slides.storyContext: Priya's mother manages the household: 2 hours cooking, 2 hours cleaning, 1 hour laundry, 1 hour shopping, 1 hour caring for Priya. That's 7 hours of unpaid work daily. She also works as a nurse (8 hours). Total: 15 hours. Priya learns: women often do double work.

slides.title: Types of Work: Primary, Secondary, Tertiary Sectors
slides.storyContext: Grandmother Savitri explains that all work falls into three categories based on what the worker does.

points.label: Primary sector (extractive industries)
points.text: Directly extracting from nature: farming, fishing, mining, forestry. Workers: farmers, fishermen, miners. About 50% of Indians work in this sector.

points.label: Secondary sector (manufacturing)
points.text: Converting raw materials into finished products: factories making clothes, cars, furniture, steel. Workers: factory workers, artisans, construction workers.

points.label: Tertiary sector (services)
points.text: Providing services: teaching, healthcare, transportation, shops, banks, government work. Workers: teachers, doctors, drivers, shopkeepers, police.

example.problem: Mohan's village has: (1) a rice farmer (primary), (2) a rice mill (secondary), (3) a grain shop (tertiary). Which worker depends on which?
example.solution: The farmer grows rice (primary). The mill owner buys rice and processes it (secondary). The shop sells processed rice (tertiary). The farmer enables the mill, which enables the shop. All three sectors are interdependent.

slides.inSimpleWords: Work is divided into three types: Primary (farming, fishing), Secondary (manufacturing), Tertiary (services like teaching, healthcare, shops).

slides.title: Example: The Rice Journey
slides.storyContext: Follow rice from Mohan's field to the dinner table.

example.problem: Mohan grows rice (primary). A mill owner buys it, husks it, and packages it (secondary). A shopkeeper sells it (tertiary). Mohan earns 100 rupees/quintal. The mill earns 50 per quintal profit. The shop earns 20 per quintal. Who benefits most?
example.solution: The mill owner (profit margin: 50%). The shopkeeper (margin: 20%). The farmer (margin: only if he had no costs—but he did). This shows why farmers often stay poor: intermediaries capture profit. This teaches economics and fairness.

slides.inSimpleWords: Products pass through many workers. Each adds value and takes a profit. Farmers often earn the least despite doing the most labor.

slides.title: Skilled and Unskilled Work; Organized and Unorganized Sectors
slides.storyContext: Mohan learns that jobs differ not just in type but in skill level, stability, and benefits.

points.label: Skilled work
points.text: Requires training or education: doctor, engineer, teacher, electrician, plumber, accountant. Usually better pay and conditions.

points.label: Unskilled work
points.text: Minimal training required: farm laborer, construction worker, street sweeper, rickshaw puller. Often lower pay and harder conditions.

points.label: Organized sector
points.text: Formal employment with contracts, fixed salary, benefits (health insurance, pension), and legal protection. Examples: government job, factory worker, teacher.

points.label: Unorganized sector
points.text: No formal contract; no benefits; work is irregular and income uncertain. Examples: street vendor, daily laborer, domestic worker. About 90% of Indians work in this sector.

example.problem: Two workers: (1) A teacher with a government contract, salary, and health insurance. (2) A street vendor who works 12 hours but has no contract and no insurance. Are they both workers?
example.solution: Yes, both are workers. But the teacher has more security. The vendor is vulnerable—one illness or injury means no income. This inequality is a major issue in India. Better wages and protections for unorganized workers are a policy goal.

slides.inSimpleWords: Some jobs are skilled (doctor, engineer) and others are unskilled (laborer). Some jobs have contracts and benefits (organized), and others don't (unorganized).

slides.title: Mohan's Friend Gets a Factory Job
slides.storyContext: Mohan's school friend Raju leaves after 10th grade to work in a textile factory. He earns 8,000/month, works 10 hours daily, no contract, no benefits. When he gets injured, there's no sick pay. Mohan realizes: unskilled workers are vulnerable.

slides.title: Child Labor: Why Kids Should Study, Not Work
slides.storyContext: Grandmother Savitri talks about a difficult topic: 'In poor families, children work in fields or factories instead of going to school. This is child labor. It's illegal and cruel.'

points.label: What is child labor?
points.text: Work done by children below 18 that prevents them from attending school or harms their health. Examples: mining, factory work, domestic servitude, sex trafficking.

points.label: Why it's wrong
points.text: Child labor steals a child's future. Without education, they stay poor and unskilled. It's exploitation.

points.label: Legal protection
points.text: Indian law (Child Labour Prohibition and Regulation Act) bans child labor. Every child has the RIGHT to education, not work.

points.label: Root cause
points.text: Poverty forces families to send children to work. Fixing child labor requires ensuring parents earn enough and families can afford school.

example.problem: A poor family needs money. Their 14-year-old son can earn 5,000/month working in a factory. Should he work or study?
example.solution: He SHOULD study. The government provides free education (Right to Free and Compulsory Education Act). The family should apply for financial aid, scholarships, or MNREGA work (adult rural jobs). The son's future is more important than immediate income.

slides.inSimpleWords: Children should study, not work. Child labor is illegal in India because every child deserves an education and a childhood.

slides.title: The School Dropout
slides.storyContext: Mohan's cousin Hari drops out of school at age 12 to help in the fields. He earns 50 rupees per day as a farm laborer. 20 years later, he's still a farm laborer, earning 300/day. If he had studied, he could be a technician earning 20,000/month. His lost opportunity cost: millions of rupees.

slides.title: Gender and Work: Why Women Are Undervalued
slides.storyContext: Priya's mother is a doctor but earns less than her male colleagues. Mohan's mother does all the housework but is called 'just a housewife.' Grandmother Savitri explains: 'Society undervalues women's work.'

points.label: The wage gap
points.text: Women are paid less than men for the same work (gender wage gap). On average, Indian women earn 20-30% less than men.

points.label: Unpaid work burden
points.text: Women do 80% of unpaid household work (cooking, childcare, washing) while also working outside. Men do half.

points.label: Career barriers
points.text: Women face discrimination in hiring, promotion, and leadership roles. They're pushed toward 'suitable' jobs (nursing, teaching).

points.label: Solutions
points.text: Equal pay laws, paid maternity leave, flexible work hours, women's education, and cultural respect for women's work.

example.problem: Priya's parents both work as doctors. Her father earns 1 lakh/month, her mother earns 85,000/month for the same job. Why?
example.solution: Discrimination based on gender. By law, this is illegal (Equal Remuneration Act, 1976). Priya's mother should report this to the labor department. Businesses that discriminate on pay face fines and penalties.

slides.inSimpleWords: Women are often paid less than men for the same work. Women also do most unpaid housework. This is unfair and must change.

slides.title: Priya's Dream and Her Mother's Advice
slides.storyContext: Priya tells her mother: 'I want to be a software engineer.' Her mother smiles: 'Study hard and aim high. Don't let anyone tell you that IT is a 'boy's field.' I've faced discrimination too. You can be what you choose.'

slides.title: The Dignity of Labor: Changing Attitudes Toward Work
slides.storyContext: In India, manual labor (farming, cleaning, construction) is often looked down upon. Grandmother Savitri challenges this: 'Every job has dignity. A farmer feeds millions. A sweeper keeps cities clean. These workers deserve respect.'

points.label: Historical caste system
points.text: In ancient India, castes were birth-based occupation groups. Certain jobs (like cleaning) were considered 'untouchable.' This legacy persists.

points.label: Modern prejudice
points.text: Today, manual workers face discrimination in education, employment, and social status. Families pressure children to avoid 'low-status' jobs.

points.label: Reality check
points.text: Farmers provide food. Cleaners prevent disease. Builders create infrastructure. Drivers transport people. Each job is essential.

points.label: Respect for all workers
points.text: A true democracy respects all workers equally. Dignity comes from honest work, not the type of work.

example.problem: A student's father is a street sweeper. At school, a classmate says, 'Your father has a dirty job.' How should the student respond?
example.solution: The student should be proud. Street sweepers keep cities clean and prevent disease. This is essential work. The classmate's ignorance is the problem, not the father's job. In a democracy, all jobs deserve respect.

slides.inSimpleWords: All work has value and dignity. A farmer, a teacher, a cleaner, a builder—all are equally important to society.

slides.title: A Worker's Rights Victory
slides.storyContext: The street sweepers in Mohan's village organize and demand better pay (now 150 rupees/day for unsafe conditions). They strike for 2 weeks. The Panchayat agrees to increase pay to 250 rupees and provide safety gear. Mohan's grandmother says: 'Workers have power when they unite. They demanded justice and won it.'

slides.title: Workers' Rights and Protections
slides.storyContext: Grandmother Savitri teaches: 'Workers should have rights: safe conditions, fair wages, no forced labor, and a voice in decisions.'

points.label: Right to safe working conditions
points.text: No child labor, no hazardous work, proper ventilation, safety equipment. Inspectors monitor factories.

points.label: Right to fair wages
points.text: Minimum wage laws ensure workers earn enough to survive. Overtime pay for extra hours.

points.label: Right to rest
points.text: Workers deserve weekly holidays, sick leave, and vacation days. No 7-day work weeks.

points.label: Right to organize
points.text: Workers can form unions to bargain collectively for better wages and conditions. Employers can't punish union members.

slides.inSimpleWords: Workers have rights: safe jobs, fair pay, rest days, and the freedom to organize for better conditions.

slides.title: Challenge: Valuing Different Workers
slides.storyContext: Mohan creates a list of different workers and their annual earnings: Farmer (2 lakhs), Factory worker (1.5 lakhs), Teacher (4 lakhs), Doctor (10 lakhs), Cleaner (60,000). Are these fair?

example.problem: Is it fair that a cleaner earns 60,000 and a doctor earns 10 lakhs? Why?
example.solution: No, this gap is unfair. The cleaner does essential work (prevents disease) but is paid little. A doctor needs more education (longer training), which justifies higher pay. But the cleaner should earn at least 2 lakhs to survive with dignity. This teaches fairness and inequality.

slides.inSimpleWords: All workers should earn enough to live with dignity. Huge wage gaps are unfair, even if some jobs require more training.

slides.title: Challenge: Child Labor in Your Community
slides.storyContext: In Mohan's village, 20 children aged 10-14 work as farm laborers instead of attending school. Their families are too poor to send them to school.

example.problem: How would you solve child labor in this village? List 3 practical steps.
example.solution: 1) Scholarship program so families don't lose income. 2) Adult wage work (MNREGA) for parents so children don't need to work. 3) Enforce school attendance laws. 4) Local awareness campaigns about education benefits. Real solutions address root causes (poverty) not just symptoms.

slides.inSimpleWords: Child labor won't stop by just banning it. You must make education affordable and parents' jobs secure.

slides.title: Mohan's Future Plan
slides.storyContext: Mohan tells his father: 'I want to study agriculture at university and return to farm but with modern technology.' His father smiles: 'That's a good dream. A farmer with education can change the village.' Mohan learns: dignity + education = opportunity.

slides.title: Education Changes Everything
slides.storyContext: Mohan's older sister studied and became a school principal. She now earns 50,000/month, has respect, and can support the family. Mohan sees: education is the most valuable investment for breaking poverty cycles.

slides.title: The Importance of Education in Work
slides.storyContext: Grandmother Savitri emphasizes: 'Education is the key to better work. More education = better jobs, higher wages, more choices.'

points.label: Skill development
points.text: Education teaches skills: reading, math, technical knowledge, critical thinking. These open doors to better jobs.

points.label: Social mobility
points.text: A farmer's child with education can become an engineer, doctor, or officer. Education breaks intergenerational poverty.

points.label: Wage premium
points.text: Each year of education increases earning potential by 5-10%. A graduate earns 3-4x more than a dropout.

points.label: Choice and freedom
points.text: Education gives workers choices. Without it, they have few options and must take any job at any wage.

slides.inSimpleWords: Education is the most powerful tool. It leads to better jobs, higher pay, and freedom to choose your career.

slides.title: Example: Paths to a Better Future
slides.storyContext: Three classmates: Asha drops out (farm labor: 300/day, no security); Ravi studies to 12th (shop clerk: 12,000/month, some security); Priya studies to degree (engineer: 50,000/month, full benefits).

example.problem: Calculate 30-year earnings: Asha (100K/year × 30 = 30 lakhs), Ravi (144K/year × 30 = 432 lakhs), Priya (600K/year × 30 = 1,800 lakhs). Why such gaps?
example.solution: Each year of education delays income but opens higher-wage paths. Priya earns less initially (school costs), but over 30 years, the wage premium compounds. This teaches delayed gratification and long-term planning.

slides.inSimpleWords: Education requires short-term sacrifice (losing income, school costs) but pays back 10x over a lifetime through better jobs and wages.

slides.title: Mohan's Reflection: Why Work Matters
slides.storyContext: Mohan sits with his grandmother. She says: 'Every job feeds a family and builds society. A farmer, a cleaner, a teacher—all are heroes. Work with pride, whatever you do.' Mohan nods: he understands now.

slides.title: Future of Work: Technology and Change
slides.storyContext: Grandmother Savitri talks about change: 'When I was young, most Indians farmed. Now many work in offices or factories. In your lifetime, new jobs will emerge—software, data science, renewable energy. Be ready to learn.'

points.label: Automation
points.text: Machines replace some manual jobs (e.g., combine harvesters replace farm labor). Workers must retrain for new skills.

points.label: New sectors emerge
points.text: Technology creates new jobs: IT, e-commerce, renewable energy. Education must evolve to train for these.

points.label: Lifelong learning
points.text: A single qualification won't last a lifetime. Workers must continuously upskill to stay relevant.

points.label: Adaptability is key
points.text: The future rewards those who can learn, adapt, and embrace change. Rigid mindsets lose opportunities.

slides.inSimpleWords: The world of work changes constantly. New jobs emerge, old ones disappear. Success requires continuous learning and adaptability.

slides.title: Priya's Career Dream
slides.storyContext: Priya dreams of coding and AI research. Mohan dreams of modernizing farming with drones and sensors. Grandmother smiles: 'In my day, we dreamed of basic jobs. You dream of skills that don't even have names yet. That's progress.'

slides.title: Work Feeds the World
slides.storyContext: Mohan now understands: every person's work sustains society. From the farmer to the teacher to his grandmother's volunteer work—all matter.

points.text: Work is any effort that produces value: paid jobs or unpaid household work.
Three sectors: Primary (farming, fishing), Secondary (manufacturing), Tertiary (services).
Jobs are skilled or unskilled; organized (with contracts) or unorganized (irregular).
Child labor is illegal. Children have the right to education, not work.
Women face wage gaps and unequal treatment in work. This must change.
All work has dignity. Every worker deserves respect and fair treatment.

slides.inSimpleWords: Work is how society sustains itself. Every person's labor contributes. Farmers, teachers, doctors, cleaners—all are essential.

subject: Social Science
title: The Economy is Everywhere: How People Produce and Trade
hook: How do villages and cities produce goods? How does food reach your plate? How does money move?

characters.name: Ananya
characters.role: A curious 12-year-old from a town in Maharashtra

characters.name: Farmer Bhagwan
characters.role: Ananya's uncle who grows sugarcane and sells it to a factory

characters.name: Mr. Patel
characters.role: A shop owner who sells goods from many local and distant producers

slides.title: Economic Activities Around Us
slides.storyContext: Ananya buys lunch at school: rice (from Punjab), curry (with vegetables from a farm near her town), chapati (wheat from Madhya Pradesh), salt (from Gujarat). In an hour, she's consumed products from 5 different regions, made by hundreds of people, bought and sold by traders. She doesn't realize it, but she's witnessing 'the economy' in action.

image.alt: Economic Activities Around Us — Economic Activities Around Us

slides.title: From Field to Table
slides.storyContext: Farmer Bhagwan grows sugarcane on his 5-acre farm. He sells it to a sugar factory 30 km away. The factory processes it into sugar and sells it to wholesalers in the city. The wholesalers sell to shop owners like Mr. Patel. Mr. Patel sells sugar to families like Ananya's. Along the way: the farmer earned income, the factory created jobs, traders made profit, shopkeeper provided service. The 'economy' is this entire chain of production and trade.

slides.title: A Day in Ananya's Economic Life
slides.storyContext: Ananya wakes up, eats breakfast (milk from a dairy farm, bread from a bakery, butter from a churning cooperative). Her mother buys vegetables at the market (from local farmers). Her father takes an auto-rickshaw to work (the driver earns a living). Ananya goes to school (the teacher is paid a salary). Everything she does involves dozens of people earning, trading, and serving. She is part of an economy without realizing it.

slides.title: What is an Economy? Production, Distribution, and Consumption
slides.storyContext: An economy is how a society organizes to produce what people need, distribute it fairly, and consume it without waste.

points.label: Production
points.text: Creating goods (food, clothes, tools) and services (teaching, healing, transportation). Farmers produce food; factories produce goods; teachers provide services.

points.label: Distribution
points.text: Moving goods from producers to consumers. Traders, transporters, shopkeepers, and wholesalers handle distribution. They earn profit.

points.label: Consumption
points.text: People using goods and services. A family consumes food, clothes, and healthcare. A business consumes raw materials.

points.label: Flow of money
points.text: Money moves in reverse: consumers pay shopkeepers, who pay wholesalers, who pay factories, who pay farmers. This circular flow sustains the economy.

example.problem: Trace the economy for a cotton shirt: (1) Who produces it? (2) How does it reach the shop? (3) How do different people earn?
example.solution: (1) Farmer grows cotton → mill spins thread → factory stitches shirt. (2) Factory sells to wholesaler → wholesaler to retailer → retailer to customer. (3) Farmer earns from cotton, mill worker earns wage, factory owner earns profit, retailer earns markup, transporter earns fee. Everyone in the chain benefits.

slides.inSimpleWords: An economy is the system of producing, distributing, and consuming goods. Money moves through this system, supporting everyone involved.

slides.title: Economy in Action: Tracing a Rice Grain
slides.storyContext: Ananya's rice grain started in a paddy field in Punjab. A farmer planted, watered, harvested, and threshed it. He sold to a wholesaler (profit: 500/sack). The wholesaler sold to a miller (profit: 100). The miller cleaned and packaged it, sold to a retailer (profit: 150). The retailer sold to Ananya's mother (profit: 50). The grain crossed 5 states, 6 transactions, and fed a family.

example.problem: A farmer sells rice at 500/sack. The retailer sells it at 800/sack (including costs). How much value was added by the wholesaler, miller, and retailer combined?
example.solution: 800 - 500 = 300/sack total value-add. Breaking down: wholesaler and transportation add 100, miller adds 100, retailer adds 100. Each step justified by effort, risk, and cost.

slides.inSimpleWords: Every product that reaches you has traveled through an economy, with each person adding value.

slides.title: Agricultural Economy: Farming and Food Production
slides.storyContext: Ananya's region is agricultural. Most people farm or work in farm-related jobs: making tools, storing grains, selling produce, processing food.

points.label: Subsistence farming
points.text: A farmer grows food mainly for his own family's consumption. No surplus to sell. Common in poorer regions.

points.label: Commercial farming
points.text: A farmer grows crops specifically for sale (sugarcane, cotton, wheat, spices). Tries to maximize yield and profit.

points.label: Cropping patterns in India
points.text: Rice and wheat (staples) in North, spices in South, cotton in Gujarat/Andhra, sugarcane in Maharashtra/Uttar Pradesh, tea in Assam/Himachal.

points.label: Agricultural support
points.text: Government helps through subsidies (cheaper seeds/fertilizer), irrigation, crop insurance, and minimum support prices (MSP).

example.problem: Farmer Bhagwan grew sugarcane but faced two problems: (1) unseasonal rain damaged 20% of the crop, (2) a factory paid less than last year. How does the government help?
example.solution: (1) Crop insurance compensates for weather damage. (2) Minimum Support Price (MSP) guarantees a floor price—if the market price drops below MSP, the government buys at MSP. This gives farmers security.

slides.inSimpleWords: Farming is a major economic activity in India. Farmers produce food and cash crops. The government helps farmers through subsidies and price support.

image.alt: Agricultural Economy: Farming and Food Production — Economic Activities Around Us

slides.title: Farmer Bhagwan's Seasons
slides.storyContext: Bhagwan's year: December-May is sugarcane season (planting, growing, harvesting). May-September is monsoon (uncertainty—too much rain causes disease, too little causes drought). He borrows money from a bank for seeds and fertilizer, repays after harvest. One bad season and he's in debt. Government MSP protects him, but so does diversification (he grows some wheat too).

slides.title: Understanding MSP (Minimum Support Price)
slides.storyContext: The government announces: MSP for sugarcane is 500/quintal. If the market price falls to 450, the government buys at 500. If the market price rises to 550, farmers sell at 550 (free market). MSP sets a floor, not a ceiling.

example.problem: Bhagwan produced 100 quintals. Market price dropped to 450. What would he earn without MSP vs. with MSP?
example.solution: Without MSP: 100 × 450 = 45,000. With MSP: 100 × 500 = 50,000. He saves 5,000 (security). This is why MSP matters for farmer livelihoods.

slides.inSimpleWords: MSP guarantees farmers a minimum price for their crops so they don't lose money in bad years.

slides.title: Industrial Economy: Manufacturing and Factories
slides.storyContext: Ananya visits a sugar factory near her town. She sees: sugarcane entering, machines processing, sugar bags being packaged and loaded onto trucks. The factory employs 200 workers, runs 24/7, and produces 500 tons of sugar daily.

points.label: What are industries?
points.text: Businesses that use machines and labor to transform raw materials into finished products. Cotton → fabric → clothes. Sugarcane → sugar.

points.label: Types of industries
points.text: Primary (extractive): mining, forestry. Secondary (manufacturing): textile mills, sugar factories, steel plants. Tertiary (services): transport, shops, schools.

points.label: Cottage industries
points.text: Small-scale, home-based production (pottery, weaving, handicrafts). Employ 1-5 people. Important for rural income.

points.label: Factory jobs and working conditions
points.text: Factories provide employment but workers often face low wages, long hours, and unsafe conditions. Labor laws protect workers' rights.

example.problem: A textile factory produces 1000 shirts daily. Its output over a year is 365,000 shirts. This creates jobs for 100 workers, income for cotton farmers, and profit for the owner. But a worker earns only 10,000/month. Is this fair?
example.solution: The worker should earn at least the minimum wage (varies by state, typically 8,000-12,000/month). If the factory profits are high, workers should share in the gains. Worker unions and labor laws push for fair wages.

slides.inSimpleWords: Factories use machines and workers to make goods from raw materials. They create jobs and income but must treat workers fairly.

slides.title: Inside the Sugar Factory
slides.storyContext: Ananya tours the factory with Bhagwan. Sugarcane arrives by truck, is crushed to extract juice, juice is boiled in massive vats to evaporate water, crystal sugar forms, and bags are filled. She meets Ramesh, who operates a machine for 12 hours, earns 400/day. She also meets the factory manager who oversees production, quality, and profit margins. Same factory, different roles, different pay.

slides.title: Factory Economy: From Cost to Profit
slides.storyContext: The sugar factory buys 1000 tons of sugarcane at 500/quintal (10,000 quintals = 100 lakh). Operating costs: labor (20 lakh), electricity (15 lakh), equipment (10 lakh), transport (5 lakh). Total: 150 lakh. Output: 300 tons of sugar, sold at 50/kg = 150 lakh.

example.problem: Revenue = 150 lakh, Costs = 150 lakh. No profit! What happened?
example.solution: The calculation is illustrative—real factories have better sugar yield, lower costs, or higher selling prices. But this shows why factories depend on efficiency. A 10% cost cut or 10% price rise changes loss to profit.

slides.inSimpleWords: Factories must manage costs carefully. Every worker, every machine, every gram of material matters to profit.

slides.title: Service Economy: Doctors, Teachers, Shops, Transportation
slides.storyContext: Services are invisible but essential. Ananya's school teacher (education), the doctor at the clinic (health), the rickshaw driver (transport), and shop owners (retail) all provide services.

points.label: What are services?
points.text: Intangible work that helps or serves people: teaching, healthcare, transportation, entertainment, banking, government. Services don't produce physical goods.

points.label: Growing importance
points.text: In developed economies, services dominate (over 70% of GDP). In India, it's 55% and growing as people get richer.

points.label: Informal services
points.text: Street vendors, auto-rickshaw drivers, domestic workers, small repair shops—these provide crucial services but are unorganized and underpaid.

points.label: Formal services
points.text: Hospitals, schools, banks, government offices—regulated, with fixed prices/fees and employee protections.

example.problem: Ananya's father uses these services in a month: doctor (500), school (5,000), bus transport (200), restaurant (1,500), barber (100). Total: 7,300 spent on services. Does services cost too much?
example.solution: Services are expensive because they require skilled people's time. A good teacher justifies their fee; a good doctor, their consultation fee. But many services (schools, buses) are subsidized by government to keep them affordable. The market price alone would exclude the poor.

slides.inSimpleWords: Services like teaching, healthcare, and transportation don't make physical goods but are crucial to society. They're a growing part of the economy.

slides.title: The Rickshaw Driver's Day
slides.storyContext: Ananya rides in an auto-rickshaw to school. The driver, Suresh, wakes at 6 AM, checks his vehicle, takes passengers all day. He earns 600/day (if he gets 8 passengers at 100-150 each, minus fuel). He has no fixed salary, no benefits, no sick leave. But his service is essential—Ananya wouldn't reach school without him.

slides.title: Comparing Formal and Informal Services
slides.storyContext: Ananya's school teacher (formal): fixed salary 30,000/month, benefits, pension, job security. Rickshaw driver (informal): 600/day, no benefits, no security, vulnerable to fuel price hikes and competition.

example.problem: Why do informal workers earn less than formal workers doing similar skilled work?
example.solution: Formal jobs have employer stability (budget), contracts, regulation. Informal workers are self-employed, variable income, no safety net. Government pushes formalization (registering informal workers, providing insurance) to improve lives.

slides.inSimpleWords: Formal jobs are stable and regulated; informal jobs are flexible but risky and often underpaid.

slides.title: Trade and Markets: How Goods Flow Between Regions
slides.storyContext: Ananya's lunch has ingredients from 5 states. Sugar from Maharashtra reaches her town through traders. A trader buys in bulk from the factory, sells to wholesalers, who sell to retailers. Each earns a markup.

points.label: Why trade?
points.text: Different regions produce different goods based on climate, soil, and resources. Trade lets people access goods from everywhere. Coffee grows in South, rice in North. Trade connects them.

points.label: Local markets
points.text: Villages and towns have weekly markets where farmers sell produce and artisans sell goods. Face-to-face trading.

points.label: Regional and national trade
points.text: Wholesale markets (mandis) aggregate goods. Traders, middlemen, and transporters move goods across states. Cities have large retail markets.

points.label: Markup and profit
points.text: Each intermediary (wholesaler, transporter, retailer) adds a markup. This is how they earn. But too many middlemen inflate prices.

example.problem: Sugarcane costs the farmer 400 per quintal. The factory pays 500 (profit: 100). The wholesaler marks up to 600 (100 profit). The retailer to 700 (100 profit). The final price to consumers is 700. Is this fair?
example.solution: It depends on services rendered. The factory processes (labor, machines). The wholesaler stores and transports (cost and risk). The retailer has a shop and serves customers. Each markup reflects their service. But if there are too many middlemen with no value-add, the final price becomes high and farmers get squeezed. The government is promoting direct-to-consumer trade (farmers selling directly in markets, cutting middlemen).

slides.inSimpleWords: Trade connects different regions. Goods flow from producers to consumers through traders and markets. Each person in the chain adds value.

image.alt: Trade and Markets: How Goods Flow Between Regions — Economic Activities Around Us

slides.title: A Day at the Mandi (Wholesale Market)
slides.storyContext: Ananya visits the agricultural mandi in her district. Hundreds of farmers arrive with produce at dawn. Middlemen (commission agents) assess quality, negotiate bulk deals, arrange transport. Wholesalers bid for goods. By 10 AM, goods are sorted, packed, and trucks leave for city retail markets. The mandi is the economic hub—controlled chaos, fortunes made and lost, farmers either satisfied or exploited.

slides.title: The Mandi Chain: From Farmer to Consumer
slides.storyContext: A farmer brings 10 tons of onions to the mandi at 15/kg = 150,000. Commission agent takes 5% (7,500). Wholesaler buys at 16/kg (160,000 - 7,500 commission to agent = 152,500 to farmer). Wholesaler sells to retailer at 18/kg. Retailer sells to consumer at 25/kg.

example.problem: Calculate profit at each step and final consumer price.
example.solution: Farmer: 150,000. Agent: 7,500. Wholesaler: 160,000 - 152,500 = 7,500 profit. Retailer: 25 × 10,000 = 250,000 - (18 × 10,000) = 70,000 profit (includes shop costs, risk). Consumer price: 25/kg. Markup seems high but each person handles risk and provides service.

slides.inSimpleWords: The mandi connects farmers to wholesale and retail markets. Each buyer adds value and takes risk.

slides.title: Money and Banking: How Transactions Work
slides.storyContext: Farmer Bhagwan sells sugarcane for 50,000 rupees. He deposits this in a bank. Later, he borrows 100,000 at 8% interest to buy fertilizer. The bank takes his deposit money from others and lends it to him. This is how money circulates in the economy.

points.label: Money's role
points.text: Money is a medium of exchange. Without it, people would barter (trade directly). Money makes transactions efficient.

points.label: Banking system
points.text: Banks accept deposits from people, pay interest, and lend to others at higher interest. The difference is their profit.

points.label: Credit and loans
points.text: Farmers borrow for seeds and fertilizer. Businesses borrow to expand. People borrow to build houses. Banks enable economic growth through lending.

points.label: Interest rates and inflation
points.text: High interest rates discourage borrowing. Low rates encourage it. The central bank (RBI in India) sets policy rates to manage the economy.

example.problem: Farmer Bhagwan borrows 100,000 at 8% interest for 1 year. How much must he repay?
example.solution: 100,000 + (100,000 x 8/100) = 100,000 + 8,000 = 108,000. If his sugarcane harvest yields 150,000 profit, he can repay easily. But if the harvest fails (weather, pest), he's in debt. This is why crop insurance exists.

slides.inSimpleWords: Banks accept money from savers and lend it to borrowers at interest. This helps businesses and individuals grow. Money circulates through the economy.

slides.title: Bhagwan's Loan
slides.storyContext: Bhagwan needs 100,000 for fertilizer and seeds. He goes to the bank with a land deed. The bank approves a loan at 8% annual interest, payable over 2 years. Monthly EMI (installment) = 4,600. If he grows good sugarcane (200 quintals at 500/quintal = 100,000), he can repay from harvest. But if prices fall or yield drops, he struggles. This is why farmers fear debt and seek government support.

slides.title: Interest and Compound Growth
slides.storyContext: Ananya's mother deposits 50,000 in a savings account at 5% annual interest. After 1 year: 50,000 + 2,500 = 52,500. After 2 years: 52,500 + 2,625 = 55,125. Money grows even if you don't work!

example.problem: How long does it take 50,000 to double at 5% interest?
example.solution: Rough estimate (Rule of 72): 72 ÷ 5 = 14.4 years. Exact: ~14.2 years. Power of compound interest—savings grow exponentially.

slides.inSimpleWords: Interest makes your money grow over time. Savings earn interest; loans cost interest. Banks are middlemen in this exchange.

slides.title: Challenge: A Complete Economic Chain
slides.storyContext: Trace the complete economic chain for a piece of clothing—from cotton production to your wardrobe. Identify: (1) All producers/workers involved, (2) All transactions and money flows, (3) All services provided.

example.problem: A cotton shirt costs 500 in a shop. Trace where this money goes. Start with: Farmer grows cotton (earns ?), Mill processes cotton (earns ?), Factory stitches shirt (earns ?), Transporter delivers (earns ?), Retailer sells (earns ?).
example.solution: One breakdown: Farmer 80, Miller 60, Factory 120, Transporter 40, Retailer markup 200 (profit after costs). Total = 500. This shows how a price is built by multiple contributors. Different markups reflect different efforts and risks.

slides.inSimpleWords: Every product involves many workers, businesses, and services. Money distributed among them is how the economy sustains millions of people.

slides.title: Challenge: Design Your Own Mandi
slides.storyContext: Imagine you're a farmer who wants to bypass middlemen and sell directly to retailers. Design a system: How would you find buyers? How would you set prices? What risks would you face?

points.label: Direct sales
points.text: Farmers' collectives are forming—cooperative groups buy from farmers at fair prices, sell to retailers, skip commission agents. Risk: organizing farmers, maintaining quality standards.

slides.inSimpleWords: Direct-to-consumer trade reduces middlemen but requires organization and coordination.

slides.title: Challenge: Economic Decision-Making
slides.storyContext: Bhagwan has 50,000 saved. He can: (A) deposit in bank at 5% (steady but slow growth), (B) invest in better seeds/fertilizer (risky but could double harvest), (C) lend to a neighbor at 10% (good return but risk of default). What should he do?

points.label: Analysis
points.text: A is safe, 2,500/year. B is risky—if harvest fails, he loses money. C is medium-risk. Most farmers choose A + B (some safe, some invested), or seek government subsidies to reduce risk of B.

slides.inSimpleWords: Economic decisions involve weighing risk, return, and security. People's choices shape the economy.

slides.title: Challenge: Spot the Economy
slides.storyContext: Look at your daily routine—sleeping, eating, going to school, playing. For each activity, list: (1) Who produced it? (2) Who transported it? (3) Who sold it? (4) Who earned money?

points.label: Example: Breakfast
points.text: Milk: Dairy farmer produced, transport company delivered, shopkeeper sold. Eggs: Farmer raised chickens, shopkeeper sold. Bread: Baker made, shopkeeper sold. All earn.

slides.inSimpleWords: Every moment of your day, the economy is working behind the scenes.

slides.title: Global Economy Connected to You
slides.storyContext: Ananya's new shoes: rubber from Malaysia, stitching in Vietnam, shipped to Mumbai, sold in her local shop. One pair of shoes involves millions of economic transactions across continents and weeks.

example.problem: A pair of shoes costs 1,500 in a shop. Estimate costs: factory labor, materials, shipping, wholesale markup, retail profit.
example.solution: Materials: 300, labor: 150, shipping: 50, factory profit: 100, wholesaler: 200, retailer: 800 profit (includes rent, staff, risk). The global supply chain is complex but the principle is same: value adds at each step.

slides.inSimpleWords: Modern economies are global—products travel far, and money flows through many countries.

slides.title: The Economy is Everywhere
slides.storyContext: Ananya now sees that every meal, every object, and every service is part of a vast economic web. Farmers, factories, traders, shopkeepers, and service providers all connect.

points.text: An economy produces, distributes, and consumes goods and services.
Agricultural economy: farming is a major sector, supported by government subsidies and MSP.
Industrial economy: factories transform raw materials into finished goods and employ workers.
Service economy: teachers, doctors, transporters, shopkeepers provide essential services.
Trade and markets connect regions. Traders, wholesalers, and retailers facilitate exchange.
Money and banking enable transactions and help businesses and people grow.

slides.inSimpleWords: The economy is everywhere—in food, clothes, schools, hospitals, shops. It works because millions of people produce, trade, and serve each other.

subject: Mathematics
title: Raj's Geometry Adventure
hook: Raj discovers lines and angles hidden in his apartment building.

characters.name: Raj
characters.role: curious student

characters.name: Meera
characters.role: math mentor

slides.title: Raj's Geometry Adventure
slides.storyContext: Raj looks out his window and sees the edges of buildings, the horizon line, the sun's rays. He realizes everything around him has lines and angles. His friend Meera shows him that geometry is not just on paper—it's everywhere.

image.alt: The Discovery — Lines and Angles

slides.title: The Discovery
slides.storyContext: Raj looks out his window and sees the edges of buildings. Meera points out that edges are really lines.
slides.inSimpleWords: Lines are straight paths that go on forever.

image.alt: The Discovery — Lines and Angles

slides.title: What is a Line?
slides.storyContext: Meera draws a line on paper with a ruler. She explains that a line has no endpoints and goes on infinitely.

points.label: Definition
points.text: A line is a straight path with no endpoints, extending infinitely in both directions.

slides.inSimpleWords: A line never ends, it keeps going forever both ways.

image.alt: What is a Line? — Lines and Angles

slides.title: Lines Everywhere
slides.storyContext: Meera shows Raj lines in nature: a horizon line (sky meets earth), a road stretching into distance, a train track. She explains that while these look finite, in geometry they are infinite.
slides.inSimpleWords: Lines are all around us, though we see only segments of them.

slides.title: Line Segment and Ray
slides.storyContext: Raj sees the edge of his table (line segment) and the beam of sunlight (ray) coming through the window.

points.label: Line Segment
points.text: A line segment has two endpoints. Example: the edge of Raj's desk.

points.label: Ray
points.text: A ray has one starting point and extends infinitely in one direction. Example: sunlight from a window.

slides.inSimpleWords: A segment has two ends, a ray has one starting point.

image.alt: Line Segment and Ray — Lines and Angles

slides.title: Measuring Line Segments
slides.storyContext: Raj measures the edge of his table: 1.5 meters. The table leg: 0.75 meters. A pencil: 19 cm. Each is a line segment with two endpoints.

example.problem: Raj's bookshelf has 3 shelves. Each shelf is 2 meters long. If he places books along 1.5 meters of each shelf, how much empty space is there per shelf?
example.solution: Empty space = 2 - 1.5 = 0.5 meters per shelf. Total empty = 0.5 × 3 = 1.5 meters. Line segment measurement applied to real objects.

slides.inSimpleWords: Line segments are the measurable parts of lines—they have length.

slides.title: What is an Angle?
slides.storyContext: Meera opens a book like a door hinge. She says the opening between the pages is an angle.

points.label: Angle
points.text: An angle is formed when two rays meet at a common point called the vertex.

slides.inSimpleWords: An angle is the space between two rays meeting at a point.

image.alt: What is an Angle? — Lines and Angles

slides.title: Angles in Raj's Room
slides.storyContext: Meera asks Raj to find angles: the corner of his desk (90°), the opening of a notebook, the corner of a door frame. Every angle has a vertex (corner) and two rays (sides).
slides.inSimpleWords: Angles are measured by how much the two rays open.

slides.title: Types of Angles
slides.storyContext: Raj measures different angles at home: the door (90°), a clock hand position (45°), and a stretched rope (180°).

example.problem: Classify these angles: 35°, 90°, 120°, 180°
example.solution: 35° is acute (less than 90°), 90° is right, 120° is obtuse (between 90° and 180°), 180° is straight.

slides.inSimpleWords: Acute angles are small, right angles are corners, obtuse are wide.

image.alt: Types of Angles — Lines and Angles

slides.title: Classifying Angles: Complete Reference
slides.storyContext: A comprehensive guide: Acute (0-90°), Right (exactly 90°), Obtuse (90-180°), Straight (exactly 180°), Reflex (180-360°).

example.solution: 45° acute, 90° right, 120° obtuse, 180° straight, 270° reflex.

slides.inSimpleWords: Every angle fits into one category based on its degree measure.

slides.title: Measuring Angles
slides.storyContext: Meera teaches Raj to use a protractor to measure the angle formed by the book pages.

points.label: Protractor
points.text: A protractor is a tool to measure angles. Place the center on the vertex and read the degree marking.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use a protractor to measure angles in degrees.

image.alt: Measuring Angles — Lines and Angles

slides.title: Using a Protractor
slides.storyContext: Meera shows Raj step-by-step: (1) Place the center dot of the protractor on the angle's vertex. (2) Align one ray with the 0° line. (3) Read where the second ray crosses the scale. Raj practices measuring angles in his homework.
slides.inSimpleWords: A protractor is like a ruler for angles.

slides.title: Finding Angles Around You
slides.storyContext: Raj finds angles in his room: corner of floor (90°), clock showing 3:00 (90°), open notebook (varies).

example.problem: What angle does a clock hand make at 3:00 and 6:00?
example.solution: At 3:00, the angle is 90°. At 6:00, the angle is 180°.

slides.inSimpleWords: Clock hands make different angles at different times.

image.alt: Finding Angles Around You — Lines and Angles

slides.title: Clock Angles: A Pattern
slides.storyContext: Clock hands move: hour hand (0.5° per minute), minute hand (6° per minute). At 3:00, they form 90°. At 6:00, they form 180°.

example.problem: What angle do clock hands make at 9:00?
example.solution: At 9:00, hour hand points to 9, minute hand points to 12. Angle = 90°.

slides.inSimpleWords: Angles on a clock follow a pattern—every hour is 30° apart.

slides.title: Complementary and Supplementary Angles
slides.storyContext: Two angles can relate: complementary if they add to 90°, supplementary if they add to 180°. Example: 30° and 60° are complementary.

points.label: Complementary
points.text: Two angles that sum to 90°. Example: 35° + 55° = 90°.

points.label: Supplementary
points.text: Two angles that sum to 180°. Example: 120° + 60° = 180°.

slides.inSimpleWords: Complementary angles 'complete' a right angle; supplementary angles 'complete' a straight line.

slides.title: Finding Missing Angles
slides.storyContext: Raj sees two angles next to each other on a line. One is 60°. What is the other if they're supplementary?

example.problem: If angle 1 is 60° and angle 1 + angle 2 = 180°, find angle 2.

slides.inSimpleWords: If two angles are supplementary and you know one, you can find the other.

slides.title: Angle Hunt
slides.storyContext: Meera challenges Raj to find and classify 5 angles in his home.

points.label: Challenge
points.text: Find angles at home: door frame (90°), pencil box lid, scissors opening, window corners.

slides.inSimpleWords: Look around and name the angles you see.

image.alt: Angle Hunt — Lines and Angles

slides.title: Vertically Opposite Angles
slides.storyContext: When two lines cross, they form 4 angles. The angles opposite each other (across the vertex) are equal. Raj draws an X and measures: both top angles are 70°, both bottom angles are 110°.

example.problem: Two lines cross. One angle is 50°. What are the other three angles?
example.solution: Opposite angle: 50°. Adjacent angles: 180° - 50° = 130° each. The four angles are 50°, 130°, 50°, 130°.

slides.inSimpleWords: Opposite angles are equal; adjacent angles are supplementary.

slides.title: Parallel and Intersecting Lines
slides.storyContext: Railway tracks never meet (parallel). Roads at an intersection cross (intersecting). Meera draws parallel lines and shows how a line cutting both creates equal angles.

points.label: Parallel
points.text: Lines that never meet, no matter how far they extend.

points.label: Intersecting
points.text: Lines that cross at a point.

points.label: Perpendicular
points.text: Lines that intersect at 90°.

slides.inSimpleWords: Lines can be parallel (never meet), intersecting (cross), or perpendicular (cross at right angles).

slides.title: Transversal and Angles
slides.storyContext: A transversal is a line cutting two parallel lines. Raj notices that the angles formed follow patterns: corresponding angles are equal, alternate angles are equal. Geometry has hidden symmetries.
slides.inSimpleWords: When a line cuts two parallel lines, angles follow predictable patterns.

slides.title: Angles Made by a Transversal
slides.storyContext: Two parallel railway tracks are cut by a road (transversal). The angles formed at each track are related. If the angle at track 1 is 60°, then the corresponding angle at track 2 is also 60°.

example.problem: A transversal cuts two parallel lines. One angle is 75°. Find the other angles.
example.solution: Corresponding angle: 75°. Alternate angle: 75°. Adjacent angle: 180° - 75° = 105°. All angles are either 75° or 105°.

slides.inSimpleWords: Parallel lines cut by a transversal create angles with predictable relationships.

slides.title: Challenge: Angle Construction
slides.storyContext: Draw a 45° angle using a protractor, then draw its complementary angle. Verify they sum to 90°.

points.label: Steps
points.text: Use protractor to mark 45°, then 90° - 45° = 45°. Both angles are equal (complementary).

slides.inSimpleWords: You can construct angles by understanding how they relate to 90° and 180°.

slides.title: Challenge: Real-World Angle Problems
slides.storyContext: A ladder leans against a wall, forming a 60° angle with the ground. What angle does it make with the wall?

points.label: Solution
points.text: The ladder, wall, and ground form a right angle (90°). If ladder-ground = 60°, then ladder-wall = 90° - 60° = 30°.

slides.inSimpleWords: Angles in triangles and real-world scenarios follow mathematical rules.

slides.title: Challenge: Spot All Angles at Home
slides.storyContext: Find 10 angles in your home, measure each with a protractor or estimate, and classify them (acute, right, obtuse, straight).

points.label: Examples
points.text: Door corners (90°), window opening (varies), corner of notebook (90°), scissors opening (acute), wall-floor angle (90°).

slides.inSimpleWords: Angles are everywhere—the more you look, the more you see geometry in real life.

slides.title: Geometry in Nature
slides.storyContext: Meera shows Raj photos of geometry in nature: a spider's web (intersecting lines and angles), a honeycomb (perpendicular lines forming angles), a snowflake (angles and symmetry). Nature is full of geometry.
slides.inSimpleWords: Geometry isn't just on paper—it's in every natural and human-made object.

slides.title: Lines and Angles Review
slides.storyContext: Raj summarizes what he learned: lines never end, rays have one start, angles form between two rays.

points.label: Lines
points.text: Infinite straight paths with no endpoints.

points.label: Segments & Rays
points.text: Segments have two endpoints, rays have one.

points.label: Angles
points.text: Formed by two rays meeting at a vertex.

slides.inSimpleWords: Lines, segments, rays, and angles are the building blocks of geometry.

image.alt: Lines and Angles Review — Lines and Angles

subject: Mathematics
title: Meera's Magic Numbers
hook: Meera finds hidden patterns in numbers while organizing her school supplies.

characters.name: Meera
characters.role: pattern finder

characters.name: Raj
characters.role: curious friend

slides.title: Meera's Magic Numbers
slides.storyContext: Meera organizes her pencils, books, and erasers. She counts them, arranges them in patterns, and notices mathematical relationships. Every number has a secret: it divides, multiplies, and connects to other numbers in surprising ways.

image.alt: Numbers Everywhere — Number Play

slides.title: Numbers Everywhere
slides.storyContext: Meera counts her pencils: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10. She notices every number is made of pairs.
slides.inSimpleWords: Numbers follow patterns we can discover.

image.alt: Numbers Everywhere — Number Play

slides.title: Even and Odd Numbers
slides.storyContext: Meera arranges pencils in pairs. Some pencils pair perfectly (even), one pencil is left alone (odd).

points.label: Even Numbers
points.text: Numbers divisible by 2 with no remainder: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12...

points.label: Odd Numbers
points.text: Numbers that leave remainder 1 when divided by 2: 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11...

slides.inSimpleWords: Even numbers divide by 2 perfectly, odd numbers don't.

image.alt: Even and Odd Numbers — Number Play

slides.title: Pairing Game
slides.storyContext: Meera lines up 10 erasers (even—pairs perfectly) and 11 erasers (odd—one left over). Raj sees the pattern: even numbers always pair; odd numbers always have one left.
slides.inSimpleWords: Even and odd is about pairing.

slides.title: Identifying Even and Odd
