slides.storyContext: Meera writes numbers: 15 (ends in 5, odd), 24 (ends in 4, even), 37 (ends in 7, odd), 50 (ends in 0, even).

example.problem: Is 123 even or odd? Is 456 even or odd?
example.solution: 123 ends in 3 (odd), 456 ends in 6 (even). Last digit determines parity.

slides.inSimpleWords: Look at the last digit—if it's 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, it's even; if it's 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, it's odd.

slides.title: Finding Factors
slides.storyContext: Meera arranges 12 pencils in different rectangular groups: 2×6, 3×4, 1×12.

example.problem: Find all factors of 12.
example.solution: Factors of 12: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12 (numbers that divide 12 with no remainder).

slides.inSimpleWords: Factors are numbers that divide another number evenly.

image.alt: Finding Factors — Number Play

slides.title: Multiples
slides.storyContext: Raj notices that if 3 is a factor, then 3, 6, 9, 12, 15... are multiples of 3.

points.label: Multiple
points.text: A multiple of a number is the result of multiplying it by any whole number.

slides.inSimpleWords: Multiples are what you get when you skip-count.

image.alt: Multiples — Number Play

slides.title: Skip-Counting
slides.storyContext: Meera skip-counts by 3s: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18... by 5s: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25... Raj notices 15 appears in both—it's a common multiple.
slides.inSimpleWords: Skip-counting reveals multiples.

slides.title: Multiples and Factors Together
slides.storyContext: Meera asks: if 5 is a factor of 20, then 20 is a multiple of 5.

example.problem: List multiples of 4. Then find which numbers have 4 as a factor.
example.solution: Multiples of 4: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20... Numbers with 4 as factor: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20 (same list!).

slides.inSimpleWords: If X is a factor, then numbers it makes are multiples of X.

image.alt: Multiples and Factors Together — Number Play

slides.title: Prime and Composite
slides.storyContext: Meera groups numbers: some (like 2, 3, 5, 7) can only be divided by 1 and themselves (prime). Others (like 4, 6, 8, 9) have more factors (composite).

points.label: Prime
points.text: A number with exactly two factors: 1 and itself. Examples: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13.

points.label: Composite
points.text: A number with more than two factors. Examples: 4, 6, 8, 9, 10, 12.

slides.inSimpleWords: Prime numbers can't be divided except by 1 and themselves.

image.alt: Prime and Composite — Number Play

slides.title: Finding Prime Numbers
slides.storyContext: Raj tries dividing 7 by 2, 3, 4, 5, 6—none divide evenly. Only 1 and 7 divide 7. It's prime! He tries 9: 3 × 3 = 9, so 9 is composite.
slides.inSimpleWords: Prime numbers are 'lonely'—only 1 and themselves divide them.

slides.title: Identifying Prime Numbers
slides.storyContext: Raj tries to divide 13 by 2, 3, 4... None work. 13 is prime!

example.problem: Is 15 prime or composite?
example.solution: 15 = 3 × 5, so it has factors 1, 3, 5, 15. It is composite.

slides.inSimpleWords: Divide by small numbers; if nothing works except 1, it's prime.

image.alt: Identifying Prime Numbers — Number Play

slides.title: Prime Numbers Up to 20
slides.storyContext: Meera lists primes: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19. She notes 2 is the only even prime.

example.problem: Why is 2 the only even prime?
example.solution: Every even number > 2 is divisible by 2, so it has at least 3 factors (1, 2, itself). Therefore, no even number > 2 is prime.

slides.inSimpleWords: 2 is special—it's even and prime.

slides.title: Divisibility Rules
slides.storyContext: Meera teaches shortcuts: a number is divisible by 2 if it ends in 0, 2, 4, 6, 8; by 3 if digits sum to a multiple of 3; by 5 if it ends in 0 or 5.

points.label: Divisible by 2
points.text: Last digit is even.

points.label: Divisible by 3
points.text: Sum of digits is divisible by 3.

points.label: Divisible by 5
points.text: Ends in 0 or 5.

slides.inSimpleWords: Divisibility rules let you check division quickly without calculating.

slides.title: Using Divisibility Rules
slides.storyContext: Is 246 divisible by 3? Sum of digits: 2 + 4 + 6 = 12. 12 is divisible by 3, so 246 is divisible by 3.

example.problem: Is 135 divisible by 3 and 5?
example.solution: Divisible by 5? Ends in 5, yes. Divisible by 3? 1 + 3 + 5 = 9, divisible by 3, yes. So 135 is divisible by both.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use divisibility rules to quickly check if numbers divide evenly.

slides.title: Number Detective
slides.storyContext: Meera challenges Raj: find all prime numbers between 1 and 20, then find all multiples of 3.
slides.inSimpleWords: Use division rules to identify number patterns.

image.alt: Number Detective — Number Play

slides.title: Challenge: GCD and LCM
slides.storyContext: Meera gives Raj two numbers: 12 and 18. Find the Greatest Common Divisor (GCD) and Least Common Multiple (LCM).

points.label: Solution
points.text: Factors of 12: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12. Factors of 18: 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18. GCD = 6. Multiples of 12: 12, 24, 36... Multiples of 18: 18, 36... LCM = 36.

slides.inSimpleWords: GCD is the biggest number that divides both; LCM is the smallest multiple of both.

slides.title: HCF (Highest Common Factor) and LCM (Least Common Multiple)
slides.storyContext: Meera has 12 red pencils and 18 blue pencils. She wants to make identical bundles with no pencils left over. What's the largest bundle size? (HCF) What's the smallest number of pencils to make equal stacks of red and blue? (LCM)

points.label: HCF
points.text: The largest number that divides two numbers evenly. For 12 and 18: HCF = 6.

points.label: LCM
points.text: The smallest number divisible by two numbers. For 12 and 18: LCM = 36.

slides.inSimpleWords: HCF finds the biggest common divisor; LCM finds the smallest common multiple.

slides.title: Finding HCF and LCM
slides.storyContext: Meera finds HCF of 20 and 30: factors of 20 (1, 2, 4, 5, 10, 20), factors of 30 (1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 10, 15, 30). Common: 1, 2, 5, 10. HCF = 10. Multiples of 20: 20, 40, 60... Multiples of 30: 30, 60, 90... LCM = 60.

example.problem: Find HCF and LCM of 15 and 25.
example.solution: Factors of 15: 1, 3, 5, 15. Factors of 25: 1, 5, 25. HCF = 5. Multiples of 15: 15, 30, 45, 60, 75... Multiples of 25: 25, 50, 75... LCM = 75.

slides.inSimpleWords: Break numbers into factors and multiples to find HCF and LCM.

slides.title: Challenge: GCD and LCM Problem
slides.storyContext: Two buses depart at the same time. One runs every 12 minutes, the other every 18 minutes. When will they depart together again? (Find LCM of 12 and 18.)

points.label: Solution
points.text: LCM(12, 18) = 36 minutes. They depart together again after 36 minutes.

slides.inSimpleWords: LCM solves real-world problems involving cycles and repetition.

slides.title: Challenge: Pattern Prediction
slides.storyContext: Meera shows Raj a sequence: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32. What's the pattern? What's the next number?

points.label: Solution
points.text: Each number is multiplied by 2. Pattern: 2^n (2 to the power of n). Next: 32 × 2 = 64.

slides.inSimpleWords: Number sequences follow rules—find the rule and predict the next number.

slides.title: Playing with Squares and Cubes
slides.storyContext: Raj notices patterns: 1×1=1, 2×2=4, 3×3=9, 4×4=16... (square numbers). Then 1×1×1=1, 2×2×2=8, 3×3×3=27... (cube numbers). Meera says these are 'perfect' numbers with special properties.
slides.inSimpleWords: Square numbers result from multiplying a number by itself; cube numbers from multiplying three times.

slides.title: Square Numbers and Cube Numbers
slides.storyContext: Meera arranges pencils in a square grid: 3×3 = 9 pencils. She builds a cube: 3×3×3 = 27 pencils. She shows Raj the first 5 squares (1, 4, 9, 16, 25) and cubes (1, 8, 27, 64, 125).

example.problem: Is 49 a square number? Is 64 both a square and a cube number?
example.solution: 49 = 7 × 7, yes. 64 = 8 × 8 (square) and 4 × 4 × 4 (cube), yes!

slides.inSimpleWords: Some numbers are special—they're both squares and cubes.

slides.title: Challenge: Mystery Number
slides.storyContext: Meera gives Raj clues: The number is even. It's divisible by 3. It's less than 30. It's a multiple of 4. What is it?

points.label: Solution
points.text: Multiples of 4 less than 30: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, 28. Even (all are). Divisible by 3: 12 or 24. Both work, but most likely 12 or 24. If it's prime-like, 24. If simpler, 12.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use divisibility rules as clues to find mystery numbers.

slides.title: Challenge: Find All Properties
slides.storyContext: Meera gives a number: 36. Find: (a) Is it even or odd? (b) Is it prime or composite? (c) All its factors. (d) Its square root. (e) Is it a multiple of 6?
slides.inSimpleWords: A single number can have many properties; list them all to understand it deeply.

slides.title: Number Play Review
slides.storyContext: Meera and Raj summarize: even/odd divide numbers, factors divide evenly, multiples come from skip-counting, primes are special.

points.label: Concepts
points.text: Even (÷2), Odd (÷2 with remainder), Factors (divide evenly), Multiples (skip-count).

points.label: Special Numbers
points.text: Prime (two factors), Composite (more than two factors).

slides.inSimpleWords: All numbers have patterns in how they divide and multiply.

image.alt: Number Play Review — Number Play

subject: Mathematics
title: The Prime Number Quest
hook: Raj and Meera discover which numbers stand alone and why they matter.

characters.name: Raj
characters.role: explorer

characters.name: Meera
characters.role: guide

slides.title: The Prime Number Quest
slides.inSimpleWords: Discover the secret numbers that build all others.

slides.title: Building Blocks
slides.storyContext: Meera shows Raj that every number is made of prime number building blocks, like atoms in chemistry.
slides.inSimpleWords: Prime numbers are nature's building blocks of all numbers.

image.alt: Building Blocks — Prime Time

slides.title: What are Prime Numbers?
slides.storyContext: Meera defines primes: numbers greater than 1 that have exactly two divisors—1 and themselves.

points.label: Prime Number
points.text: A natural number greater than 1 with exactly two divisors: 1 and itself. Examples: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11.

points.label: Composite Number
points.text: A natural number with more than two divisors. Example: 6 (divisors: 1, 2, 3, 6).

slides.inSimpleWords: Primes are numbers divisible only by 1 and themselves.

slides.title: Raj's Prime Hunt
slides.storyContext: Raj looks at small numbers: 2 is prime (only 1, 2 divide it). 3 is prime (only 1, 3). But 4 is not—1, 2, 4 all divide it. He realizes not all numbers are prime!

points.label: Key Insight
points.text: A prime is 'indivisible' except by itself and 1, like an atom.

slides.inSimpleWords: Primes stand alone; composites break apart into smaller pieces.

slides.title: Identifying Prime Numbers
slides.storyContext: Raj checks if numbers are prime: Is 7 prime? Only 1 and 7 divide it—yes! Is 9 prime? 1, 3, and 9 divide it—no!

example.problem: Is 13 prime? Check all divisors.

slides.inSimpleWords: Test if only 1 and the number itself divide it.

slides.title: Prime Factorization
slides.storyContext: Raj breaks 12 into primes: 12 = 2 × 2 × 3. He draws a tree showing how 12 splits into smaller primes.

points.label: Prime Factorization
points.text: Writing a number as a product of only prime numbers. Example: 12 = 2² × 3.

slides.inSimpleWords: Every number can be broken into prime number pieces.

image.alt: Prime Factorization — Prime Time

slides.title: The Factor Tree Mystery
slides.storyContext: Meera shows Raj why factor trees work: start at top (composite), split into two factors, keep splitting until only primes remain. Different paths lead to same prime list!

points.label: Method
points.text: Keep dividing by smallest prime until you reach primes at every branch.

slides.inSimpleWords: Factor trees always end at the same primes, no matter how you branch.

slides.title: Factor Trees
slides.storyContext: Meera and Raj draw trees for different numbers, each ending in prime leaves.

example.problem: Find prime factorization of 30.
example.solution: 30 = 2 × 15 = 2 × 3 × 5. Prime factorization: 2 × 3 × 5.

slides.inSimpleWords: Keep dividing by small primes until only primes remain.

image.alt: Factor Trees — Prime Time

slides.title: Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic
slides.storyContext: Meera explains: every number has ONE unique prime factorization, like a fingerprint.

points.label: Unique Factorization
points.text: Every composite number has exactly one prime factorization (ignoring order). Example: 60 = 2² × 3 × 5 always, never another way.

slides.inSimpleWords: Each number's prime breakdown is unique and unchangeable.

slides.title: Checking Prime Factorizations
slides.storyContext: Raj verifies: 24 = 2³ × 3. Multiply: 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 = 8 × 3 = 24. Correct!

example.problem: Verify the prime factorization of 36: 36 = 2² × 3².

slides.inSimpleWords: Multiply the prime factors to verify the original number.

slides.title: GCD and LCM
slides.storyContext: Meera finds the Greatest Common Divisor (GCD) and Least Common Multiple (LCM) using prime factors.

points.label: GCD
points.text: Greatest Common Divisor: largest number dividing both. Use shared prime factors.

points.label: LCM
points.text: Least Common Multiple: smallest number divisible by both. Use all prime factors.

slides.inSimpleWords: GCD is the biggest shared divider, LCM is the smallest common multiple.

image.alt: GCD and LCM — Prime Time

slides.title: Raj's Bus Problem
slides.storyContext: Raj and Meera notice: bus A comes every 12 minutes, bus B every 18 minutes. When do both arrive together? They use LCM to find: every 36 minutes! For dividing 24 apples and 36 oranges equally, they use GCD = 12.

points.label: Real-World Use
points.text: LCM = when events sync. GCD = how to divide equally.

slides.inSimpleWords: GCD divides fairly, LCM synchronizes repeating events.

slides.title: Finding GCD and LCM
slides.storyContext: Raj finds GCD and LCM of 12 and 18 using their prime factorizations.

example.problem: Find GCD and LCM of 12 and 18.

slides.inSimpleWords: GCD uses only shared primes, LCM uses all primes.

image.alt: Finding GCD and LCM — Prime Time

slides.title: GCD & LCM in Real Life
slides.storyContext: Meera shows uses: GCD divides equally into groups, LCM syncs repeating events.

points.label: GCD Use
points.text: Arranging 12 apples and 18 oranges into identical baskets with no leftovers.

points.label: LCM Use
points.text: Finding when two buses (one every 12 mins, one every 18 mins) leave together.

slides.inSimpleWords: GCD divides, LCM synchronizes.

slides.title: Applied GCD Problem
slides.storyContext: Raj has 24 chocolates and 36 biscuits. He wants identical gift boxes with no leftover. What's the max number of boxes?

example.problem: Find GCD(24, 36) to determine max identical boxes.
example.solution: 24 = 2³ × 3, 36 = 2² × 3². GCD = 2² × 3 = 12. So 12 boxes maximum.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use GCD to divide equally into maximum groups.

slides.title: Applied LCM Problem
slides.storyContext: Two lights blink: one every 12 seconds, one every 18 seconds. When do both blink together?

example.problem: Find LCM(12, 18) for synchronized blink time.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use LCM to find when events repeat together.

slides.title: Sieves and Prime Patterns
slides.storyContext: Meera shows the Sieve of Eratosthenes: crossing out multiples to find all primes up to 50.

points.label: Sieve Method
points.text: Cross out all multiples of each prime to find remaining primes.

points.label: Pattern
points.text: Primes become rarer as numbers get larger, but never end.

slides.inSimpleWords: Eliminate multiples to reveal all prime numbers.

image.alt: Sieves and Prime Patterns — Prime Time

slides.title: Prime Sieve Practice
slides.storyContext: Raj uses the sieve for numbers 1-30: mark 2, cross 4,6,8...; mark 3, cross 9,15,21...; mark 5, cross 25...

example.problem: Use Sieve of Eratosthenes to find primes up to 30.

slides.inSimpleWords: Mark each prime, cross out all its multiples.

image.alt: Prime Sieve Practice — Prime Time

slides.title: Special Primes and Twin Primes
slides.storyContext: Meera shows patterns: 2 is the only even prime, and some primes come in pairs (5&7, 11&13, 17&19).

points.label: Even Prime
points.text: 2 is the only even prime; all other primes are odd.

points.label: Twin Primes
points.text: Pairs of primes differing by 2. Examples: (3,5), (5,7), (11,13), (17,19).

slides.inSimpleWords: 2 is special—the only even prime. Twin primes come in pairs.

slides.title: Finding Twin Primes
slides.storyContext: Raj searches for twin primes up to 50. He finds: (3,5), (5,7), (11,13), (17,19), (29,31), (41,43).

example.problem: List all twin prime pairs less than 50.

slides.inSimpleWords: Find consecutive odd primes that differ by 2.

slides.title: Prime Power Challenge
slides.storyContext: Meera asks Raj to find prime factorizations of 36 and 45, then their GCD.

points.label: Challenge
points.text: 36 = 2² × 3², 45 = 3² × 5. GCD = 9. Verify by division.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use prime factors to solve GCD and LCM puzzles.

image.alt: Prime Power Challenge — Prime Time

slides.title: Complex Factorization Challenge
slides.storyContext: Raj tackles a harder number: factor 120 completely and express it in exponential form.

example.problem: Find the prime factorization of 120 in exponential form.

slides.inSimpleWords: Break the number step by step until only primes remain.

slides.title: Prime Gaps and Distribution
slides.storyContext: Meera explains why gaps between primes vary: 2→3 (gap 1), 3→5 (gap 2), 5→7 (gap 2), 7→11 (gap 4).

points.label: Prime Gap
points.text: The difference between consecutive primes. Example: gap between 11 and 13 is 2.

points.label: Density
points.text: Primes become less frequent as numbers grow (fewer in 100-200 than in 1-100).

slides.inSimpleWords: Gaps between primes grow larger as numbers increase.

slides.title: Analyzing Prime Gaps

example.problem: Find the gap between 29 and 37.
example.solution: Primes: 29, 31, 37. Gaps are 2 and 6. Largest gap in this range is 6.

slides.inSimpleWords: Count how many numbers separate consecutive primes.

slides.title: Divisibility Tests for Primes
slides.storyContext: Meera teaches shortcuts to check divisibility without division: by 2 (even?), by 3 (digits sum divisible by 3?), by 5 (ends in 0 or 5?).

points.label: Quick Tests
points.text: Divisible by 2: even. By 3: digit sum divisible by 3. By 5: ends in 0 or 5.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use quick rules to check if primes divide a number.

slides.title: Using Divisibility Tests
slides.storyContext: Raj checks 315: Ends in 5 (divisible by 5). Digits: 3+1+5=9 (divisible by 3). So 315 is divisible by 3 and 5.

example.problem: Check if 315 is divisible by 2, 3, 5, 11.
example.solution: 315 is odd (not by 2). Digits sum to 9 (divisible by 3). Ends in 5 (divisible by 5). Check 11: 3-1+5=7 (not divisible by 11).

slides.inSimpleWords: Apply quick tests instead of long division.

slides.title: Finding LCM of Three Numbers
slides.storyContext: Meera asks: find LCM of 12, 18, and 20 using prime factorization.
slides.inSimpleWords: Use highest power of each prime factor.

slides.title: Real-World Prime Factorization
slides.storyContext: Raj needs to pack 84 pencils and 126 erasers into identical kits. What's the maximum kit size?

example.problem: Find GCD(84, 126) for maximum kit size.
example.solution: 84 = 2² × 3 × 7, 126 = 2 × 3² × 7. GCD = 2 × 3 × 7 = 42. So 42 items per kit maximum.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use GCD to find the largest equal groups.

slides.title: Goldbach's Conjecture
slides.storyContext: Meera mentions an unsolved mystery: every even number > 2 is the sum of two primes. Example: 10 = 5+5, 12 = 5+7.

points.label: Goldbach's Conjecture
points.text: Every even number greater than 2 can be expressed as the sum of two primes.

points.label: Unsolved
points.text: True for all tested numbers up to trillions, but no proof yet exists.

slides.inSimpleWords: Mathematicians still wonder if every even number is two primes added.

slides.title: Prime Time Review
slides.storyContext: Raj and Meera recap: all numbers are built from primes, factor trees show the structure, GCD/LCM solve real problems.

points.label: Prime Factorization
points.text: Every number = unique product of primes.

points.label: GCD & LCM
points.text: Essential for fractions and problem-solving.

points.label: Sieves & Patterns
points.text: Ancient method to find primes; patterns exist but primes never end.

points.label: Real Uses
points.text: Cryptography, equal distribution, synchronized events.

slides.inSimpleWords: Primes are nature's number building blocks.

image.alt: Prime Time Review — Prime Time

subject: Mathematics
title: Measuring Meera's Garden
hook: Meera plans to fence and paint her garden, learning perimeter and area.

characters.name: Meera
characters.role: gardener

characters.name: Raj
characters.role: helper

slides.title: Measuring Meera's Garden
slides.inSimpleWords: Learn how to fence the boundary and paint the inside.

slides.title: Garden Plans
slides.storyContext: Meera wants to fence her rectangular garden and paint the ground. She needs to know how much fence (perimeter) and paint (area).
slides.inSimpleWords: Perimeter measures the distance around, area measures the space inside.

image.alt: Garden Plans — Perimeter and Area

slides.title: What is Perimeter?
slides.storyContext: Raj walks around Meera's garden boundary. The total distance he walks is the perimeter.

points.label: Perimeter
points.text: Sum of all side lengths around a closed shape.

points.label: Units
points.text: Measured in linear units: cm, m, km, inches, feet.

slides.inSimpleWords: Perimeter is the distance around the outside of a shape.

image.alt: What is Perimeter? — Perimeter and Area

slides.title: Walking the Garden Edge
slides.storyContext: Raj walks 8m along one side, 5m along another, 8m on the third, and 5m on the last—that's 26m total! Meera realizes she needs 26m of fencing to go around the whole garden.

points.label: Insight
points.text: Perimeter = the complete 'path' around any closed shape.

slides.inSimpleWords: Trace the whole boundary—that's the perimeter.

slides.title: Perimeter of Rectangles
slides.storyContext: Meera's garden is 8 meters long and 5 meters wide. How much fencing does she need?

example.problem: Find perimeter of a rectangle with length 8 m and width 5 m.
example.solution: Perimeter = 2(length + width) = 2(8 + 5) = 2(13) = 26 meters.

slides.inSimpleWords: Perimeter of rectangle = 2 × (length + width).

image.alt: Perimeter of Rectangles — Perimeter and Area

slides.title: Perimeter of Different Shapes
slides.storyContext: Raj notices the garden border has different shapes: straight sides (rectangle), curved (circle), slanted (triangle).

points.label: Square
points.text: Perimeter = 4 × side.

points.label: Triangle
points.text: Perimeter = side₁ + side₂ + side₃.

points.label: Circle
points.text: Perimeter (circumference) = 2πr (where r is radius).

slides.inSimpleWords: Add all sides for perimeter; circle uses radius and π.

slides.title: Perimeter of Squares and Triangles
slides.storyContext: Meera marks a square flower bed (side 6m) and triangular bed (sides 5m, 6m, 7m).

example.problem: Find perimeter of a square with side 6m and a triangle with sides 5m, 6m, 7m.
example.solution: Square: P = 4 × 6 = 24m. Triangle: P = 5 + 6 + 7 = 18m.

slides.inSimpleWords: Multiply for squares, add all sides for triangles.

slides.title: What is Area?
slides.storyContext: Meera measures how many square meter tiles fit in her garden. Each tile is 1m × 1m.

points.label: Area
points.text: Measure of space inside a closed shape, measured in square units.

points.label: Square Units
points.text: cm², m², km², square inches, square feet.

slides.inSimpleWords: Area is how much space covers the shape.

image.alt: What is Area? — Perimeter and Area

slides.title: Tiling the Garden
slides.storyContext: Meera and Raj lay down 1m×1m tiles in rows: 8 tiles in a row, 5 rows. That's 8×5 = 40 tiles total! Each tile is 1 square meter, so the garden is 40 square meters.

points.label: Key Idea
points.text: Area = how many unit squares fit inside the shape.

slides.inSimpleWords: Count the square units that cover the whole shape.

slides.title: Area of Rectangles
slides.storyContext: Meera's garden 8m × 5m is covered by 40 square tiles, each 1m × 1m.

example.problem: Find area of the same garden (8 m × 5 m).
example.solution: Area = length × width = 8 × 5 = 40 square meters.

slides.inSimpleWords: Area of rectangle = length × width.

image.alt: Area of Rectangles — Perimeter and Area

slides.title: Perimeter vs. Area
slides.storyContext: Meera notices: two gardens with same perimeter can have different areas, and vice versa.

points.label: Same Perimeter, Different Area
points.text: 2×3 rectangle: P=10, A=6. 1×4 rectangle: P=10, A=4.

points.label: Independence
points.text: Perimeter and area are independent properties.

slides.inSimpleWords: Shapes can have same perimeter but different areas.

slides.title: Comparing Perimeter and Area
slides.storyContext: Raj creates two garden plans: 6m×4m and 5m×5m. Which has more fence? Which has more space?

example.problem: Compare 6m×4m rectangle (P, A) with 5m×5m square (P, A).
example.solution: Rectangle: P=20m, A=24m². Square: P=20m, A=25m². Same perimeter, square has more area!

slides.inSimpleWords: Same perimeter can yield different areas.

slides.title: Area of Other Shapes
slides.storyContext: Raj notices different garden shapes: triangular flower beds and circular fountain.

points.label: Triangle Area
points.text: Area = ½ × base × height.

points.label: Circle Area
points.text: Area = π × r² (where r is radius).

slides.inSimpleWords: Different shapes have different area formulas.

image.alt: Area of Other Shapes — Perimeter and Area

slides.title: Mixed Shapes
slides.storyContext: A triangular flower bed has base 6m and height 4m. What is its area?

example.problem: Find area of triangle with base 6 m and height 4 m.
example.solution: Area = ½ × 6 × 4 = ½ × 24 = 12 square meters.

slides.inSimpleWords: Triangle area is half of the rectangle with same base and height.

image.alt: Mixed Shapes — Perimeter and Area

slides.title: Circle Perimeter and Area
slides.storyContext: Meera finds a circular fountain in the center. Raj measures radius = 2m. How much rope to wrap it? How much paint for the ground?

points.label: Circumference
points.text: C = 2πr or C = πd (diameter d = 2r).

points.label: Area
points.text: A = πr².

points.label: Note on π
points.text: π ≈ 3.14 or use as symbol.

slides.inSimpleWords: Circle perimeter uses 2πr, area uses πr².

slides.title: Circle Circumference and Area
slides.storyContext: Meera's fountain: radius = 2m. How much rope? How much paint?

example.problem: Find circumference and area of a circle with radius 2m (use π ≈ 3.14).

slides.inSimpleWords: Use radius to find circumference and area of circles.

slides.title: Area of Irregular Shapes
slides.storyContext: The garden has an L-shaped section. Raj breaks it into two rectangles and adds their areas.

points.label: Composite Shapes
points.text: Break irregular shapes into simple shapes (rectangles, triangles) and add areas.

slides.inSimpleWords: Split complex shapes into simpler ones, then add areas.

slides.title: L-Shaped Area
slides.storyContext: An L-shaped garden can be split into two rectangles: 8m×3m and 5m×2m. What's the total area?

example.problem: Find area of L-shaped garden split into 8m×3m and 5m×2m rectangles.
example.solution: Area₁ = 8 × 3 = 24m². Area₂ = 5 × 2 = 10m². Total = 24 + 10 = 34m².

slides.inSimpleWords: Add areas of parts to get the whole.

slides.title: Parallelogram and Trapezoid Areas
slides.storyContext: Meera discovers slanted shapes: parallelograms (Area = base × height) and trapezoids (Area = ½(b₁+b₂)×h).

points.label: Parallelogram
points.text: Area = base × height (height is perpendicular to base).

points.label: Trapezoid
points.text: Area = ½ × (base₁ + base₂) × height.

slides.inSimpleWords: Slanted shapes have formulas that adjust for non-perpendicular sides.

slides.title: Parallelogram and Trapezoid Problems
slides.storyContext: Raj calculates: parallelogram with base 6m, height 4m; trapezoid with bases 5m & 7m, height 3m.

example.problem: Find area of parallelogram (base 6m, height 4m) and trapezoid (bases 5m & 7m, height 3m).
example.solution: Parallelogram: A = 6 × 4 = 24m². Trapezoid: A = ½(5+7)×3 = ½×12×3 = 18m².

slides.inSimpleWords: Use base and height for parallelograms; average bases for trapezoids.

slides.title: Garden Redesign
slides.storyContext: Meera wants to expand her garden or change its shape. Raj calculates new perimeter and area.

points.label: Challenge
points.text: If Meera makes the garden 10m × 6m, new perimeter = 32m, new area = 60 sq.m.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use formulas to compare different garden sizes.

image.alt: Garden Redesign — Perimeter and Area

slides.title: Maximum Area Challenge
slides.storyContext: Meera has 40m of fencing. Which shape—rectangle, square, or circle—fits the most area?

example.problem: With 40m fencing, find area for square (P=40), rectangle 12×8 (P=40), and circle (P=40).
example.solution: Square (10×10): A=100m². Rectangle (12×8): A=96m². Circle (C=40, r≈6.37): A≈127.7m². Circle wins!

slides.inSimpleWords: Among same perimeter, circle has largest area.

slides.title: Fencing and Painting Budget
slides.storyContext: Fencing costs Rs. 50/m, paint costs Rs. 10/m². Meera's 8m×5m garden costs how much total?

example.problem: Calculate total cost: fencing (P=26m @ Rs.50/m) + paint (A=40m² @ Rs.10/m²).
example.solution: Fencing = 26 × 50 = Rs.1300. Paint = 40 × 10 = Rs.400. Total = Rs.1700.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use perimeter for cost of border, area for cost of inside.

slides.title: Scale and Unit Conversion
slides.storyContext: Meera's blueprint is in cm but real garden is in m. Raj converts: 1m = 100cm, so 1m² = 10,000cm².

points.label: Length Conversion
points.text: 1m = 100cm, 1km = 1000m. Perimeters scale linearly.

points.label: Area Conversion
points.text: 1m² = 10,000cm², 1km² = 1,000,000m². Areas scale by square.

slides.inSimpleWords: Length doubles means perimeter doubles; area quadruples.

slides.title: Unit Conversion Practice
slides.storyContext: Meera's blueprint: garden 40cm×25cm. Real size: 8m×5m. Verify scaling.

example.problem: If blueprint is 40cm×25cm and real is 8m×5m, what's the scale?

slides.inSimpleWords: Compare dimensions to find the scale factor.

slides.title: Mixed Shapes Garden Layout
slides.storyContext: Meera's complex garden has a rectangular section (10m×6m), semicircular flower bed (r=2m), and triangular herb garden (base 4m, height 3m). Find total area.

example.problem: Find total area: rectangle 10×6, semicircle r=2, triangle base 4 height 3.
example.solution: Rectangle: 10×6=60. Semicircle: ½π×2²≈6.28. Triangle: ½×4×3=6. Total≈72.28m².

slides.inSimpleWords: Add areas of different shapes to find total garden space.

slides.title: Real-World Perimeter and Area
slides.storyContext: Raj discovers perimeter matters for fencing cost, area for water/fertilizer. A square uses least fence for max area!

points.label: Optimization
points.text: Among all shapes with same perimeter, a circle has max area; among polygons, a square is best.

points.label: Practical
points.text: Farmers use area for crop planning; gardeners use perimeter for fencing.

slides.inSimpleWords: Squares and circles are nature's most efficient shapes.

slides.title: Perimeter and Area Review
slides.storyContext: Meera buys fencing (perimeter) and paint (area) for her garden.

points.label: Perimeter
points.text: Sum of all sides; Rectangle = 2(l+w), Circle = 2πr.

points.label: Area
points.text: Space inside; Rectangle = l×w, Triangle = ½bh, Circle = πr².

points.label: Units
points.text: Perimeter in units (m), Area in square units (m²).

points.label: Key Insight
points.text: Same perimeter ≠ same area. Different shapes matter.

slides.inSimpleWords: Perimeter fences a garden, area paints its ground.

image.alt: Perimeter and Area Review — Perimeter and Area

subject: Mathematics
title: Sharing Pizza with Fractions
hook: Raj and Meera share a pizza and learn fractions the fun way.

characters.name: Raj
characters.role: pizza lover

characters.name: Meera
characters.role: fraction teacher

slides.title: Sharing Pizza with Fractions
slides.inSimpleWords: Learn how to divide a pizza fairly and understand parts.

slides.title: Pizza Division
slides.storyContext: A pizza arrives. Raj cuts it into 8 equal slices. He eats 3 slices. Meera says he ate 3/8 of the pizza.
slides.inSimpleWords: Fractions show parts of a whole.

image.alt: Pizza Division — Fractions

slides.title: Understanding Fractions
slides.storyContext: Meera points out: 3 slices (numerator) out of 8 total slices (denominator).

points.label: Numerator
points.text: Top number: how many parts we have.

points.label: Denominator
points.text: Bottom number: how many equal parts the whole is divided into.

slides.inSimpleWords: Numerator is top (parts chosen), denominator is bottom (parts total).

image.alt: Understanding Fractions — Fractions

slides.title: The Pizza Slicing Mystery
slides.storyContext: Raj wonders: when Meera cuts the same pizza into 4 slices instead of 8, does the fraction change? She explains—1/2 is 1/2, whether it's 4 slices out of 8 or 2 slices out of 4!

points.label: Key Insight
points.text: The SAME piece can be written as many different fractions.

slides.inSimpleWords: Different fractions can mean the same amount of pizza.

slides.title: Reading and Writing Fractions
slides.storyContext: Meera shows Raj how to read fractions: 3/8 is 'three-eighths', 1/2 is 'one-half', 5/6 is 'five-sixths'.

example.problem: Write and read: Raj ate 3 out of 8 slices, Meera ate 2 out of 8.
example.solution: Raj: 3/8 (three-eighths). Meera: 2/8 (two-eighths).

slides.inSimpleWords: Say numerator, then denominator name (thirds, fourths, eighths).

slides.title: Types of Fractions
slides.storyContext: Raj notices different slicing: 1/4 (one quarter), 1/2 (one half), 3/8 (three eighths), 9/8 (more than whole).

points.label: Proper Fraction
points.text: Numerator < Denominator. Less than 1. Examples: 2/5, 3/8.

points.label: Improper Fraction
points.text: Numerator ≥ Denominator. At least 1. Examples: 5/5, 9/8.

points.label: Mixed Number
points.text: Whole number + proper fraction. Example: 1 3/8.

slides.inSimpleWords: Proper < 1, improper ≥ 1. Mixed numbers combine whole + proper.

image.alt: Types of Fractions — Fractions

slides.title: Two Pizzas and One More
slides.storyContext: Raj orders 2 pizzas, and they eat 3 slices from another pizza cut into 8. That's 2 and 3/8 pizzas total! Meera shows how to convert: 2 3/8 = 19/8.

points.label: Conversion
points.text: Mixed number (whole + proper) = improper fraction (parts over denominator).

slides.inSimpleWords: 1 3/8 means 1 whole pizza plus 3 slices from another.

slides.title: Converting Between Mixed and Improper
slides.storyContext: Raj eats 1 3/8 pizzas (one and three-eighths). How many eighths total? 8/8 + 3/8 = 11/8.

example.problem: Convert 1 3/8 to improper fraction and 11/8 to mixed number.

slides.inSimpleWords: Mixed = improper by multiplying whole by denominator and adding numerator.

slides.title: Equivalent Fractions
slides.storyContext: Meera cuts two pizzas differently: one into 4 slices (Raj eats 2 = 2/4), another into 8 slices (Meera eats 4 = 4/8). They ate the same amount!

points.label: Equivalent
points.text: Fractions that represent the same part of a whole. Example: 2/4 = 4/8.

points.label: Rule
points.text: Multiply or divide numerator and denominator by the same number.

slides.inSimpleWords: Different fractions can mean the same amount.

image.alt: Equivalent Fractions — Fractions

slides.title: Finding Equivalent Fractions
slides.storyContext: Meera shows: 2/4 = 4/8 = 6/12 all equal 1/2. Raj multiplies top and bottom by 3 to verify.

example.problem: Find three equivalent fractions for 2/5.
example.solution: 2/5 = 4/10 = 6/15 = 8/20 (multiply by 2, 3, 4 respectively).

slides.inSimpleWords: Multiply top and bottom by same number to get equivalent.

slides.title: Simplifying Fractions
slides.storyContext: Raj wonders if 6/9 can be simplified. Meera divides both by 3: 6/9 = 2/3.

points.label: Simplify
points.text: Divide numerator and denominator by their GCD to get lowest terms.

points.label: Lowest Terms
points.text: When numerator and denominator share no common factors except 1.

slides.inSimpleWords: Divide numerator and denominator by their GCD.

image.alt: Simplifying Fractions — Fractions

slides.title: Simplifying Practice
slides.storyContext: Raj simplifies several fractions: 12/16, 15/25, 8/12.

example.problem: Simplify 12/16 to lowest terms.
example.solution: GCD(12,16) = 4. 12/16 = 3/4 (divide top and bottom by 4).

slides.inSimpleWords: Find GCD and divide both by it.

slides.title: Comparing Fractions
slides.storyContext: Meera asks: who ate more—Raj (3/8) or Meera (2/5)? They find common denominator to compare.

points.label: Same Denominator
points.text: Larger numerator = larger fraction. 3/8 vs 4/8: 4/8 is bigger.

points.label: Different Denominators
points.text: Convert to common denominator, then compare numerators.

slides.inSimpleWords: Same denominator: compare numerators. Different: find common denominator.

slides.title: Comparing Fractions with Different Denominators

example.problem: Compare 3/8 and 2/5.

slides.inSimpleWords: Convert to common denominator, compare numerators.

slides.title: Adding and Subtracting Fractions
slides.storyContext: Raj ate 1/4 pizza, Meera ate 2/4. Together they ate 1/4 + 2/4 = 3/4.

points.label: Same Denominator
points.text: Add/subtract numerators, keep denominator: 1/4 + 2/4 = 3/4.

slides.inSimpleWords: Same denominator: add/subtract tops, keep bottom same.

image.alt: Adding and Subtracting Fractions — Fractions

slides.title: Adding Same Denominator
slides.storyContext: Total eaten: Raj (3/8) + Meera (2/8) + friend (1/8) = 6/8. Simplify: 6/8 = 3/4.

example.solution: (3+2+1)/8 = 6/8 = 3/4 (simplified by dividing by 2).

slides.inSimpleWords: Add numerators when denominators match.

slides.title: Adding and Subtracting Different Denominators
slides.storyContext: Raj wants to add 1/3 + 1/4. Meera finds LCM(3,4) = 12: 1/3 = 4/12, 1/4 = 3/12, sum = 7/12.

points.label: Steps
points.text: Find LCM of denominators. Convert both to equivalent fractions. Add/subtract numerators.

slides.inSimpleWords: Find common denominator using LCM before adding.

image.alt: Finding Common Denominators — Fractions

slides.title: Adding Different Denominators
slides.storyContext: Meera has 1/3 pizza, Raj adds 1/4 pizza. How much total?
slides.inSimpleWords: Convert to same denominator, then add.

slides.title: Multiplying and Dividing Fractions
slides.storyContext: Meera has 3/4 pizza. She cuts it in half for dessert (multiply by 1/2). Result: 3/4 × 1/2 = 3/8.

points.label: Multiply
points.text: Multiply numerators and denominators: (a/b) × (c/d) = (a×c)/(b×d).

points.label: Divide
points.text: Multiply by reciprocal: (a/b) ÷ (c/d) = (a/b) × (d/c).

slides.inSimpleWords: Multiply across; divide by flipping second fraction.

slides.title: Multiplying Fractions
slides.storyContext: Meera has 2/3 pizza and eats 3/4 of it. How much did she eat? 2/3 × 3/4 = 6/12 = 1/2.

example.problem: Multiply 2/3 × 3/4.

slides.inSimpleWords: Multiply numerators, multiply denominators, simplify.

slides.title: Dividing Fractions
slides.storyContext: Raj has 3/4 pizza and divides it equally among 3 friends. Each gets 3/4 ÷ 3 = 3/4 × 1/3 = 1/4.
slides.inSimpleWords: Flip the divisor, then multiply.

slides.title: Pizza Math Challenge
slides.storyContext: Raj eats 3/8, Meera eats 2/8, their friend eats 1/8. What fraction remains?
slides.inSimpleWords: Use addition to find total, subtract from 1.

image.alt: Pizza Math Challenge — Fractions

slides.title: Recipe Scaling
slides.storyContext: A recipe calls for 1/2 cup flour and 1/4 cup sugar. Meera wants to double it. How much of each?

example.problem: Double the recipe: 1/2 cup flour × 2 and 1/4 cup sugar × 2.
example.solution: Flour: 1/2 × 2 = 1 cup. Sugar: 1/4 × 2 = 1/2 cup.

slides.inSimpleWords: Multiply recipe fractions by the scaling factor.

slides.title: Complex Fraction Operations
slides.storyContext: Raj calculates: 3/4 + 1/6 - 1/8. Find LCM and solve.

example.problem: Calculate 3/4 + 1/6 - 1/8.

slides.inSimpleWords: Find LCM of all denominators, convert, then add/subtract.

slides.title: Subtracting Different Denominators
slides.storyContext: Meera has 5/6 pizza, eats 1/3. How much remains? 5/6 - 1/3 = 5/6 - 2/6 = 3/6 = 1/2.

example.problem: Subtract 5/6 - 1/3.

slides.inSimpleWords: Find common denominator, convert, then subtract.

slides.title: Fractions Review
slides.storyContext: Raj and Meera finish their pizza lesson, understanding fractions deeply.

points.label: Basics
points.text: Numerator (parts chosen), Denominator (total parts), Types (proper, improper, mixed).

points.label: Operations
points.text: Simplify using GCD, add/subtract/multiply/divide using common denominators or reciprocals.

points.label: Equivalence
points.text: Same part can be written many ways; always simplify to lowest terms.

points.label: Real Use
points.text: Fractions describe sharing, measuring, cooking, time, and recipes.

slides.inSimpleWords: Fractions are ways to show parts of a whole.

image.alt: Fractions Review — Fractions

subject: Mathematics
title: Collecting School Survey Data
hook: Raj and Meera survey classmates to learn how to collect and display data.

characters.name: Raj
characters.role: data collector

characters.name: Meera
characters.role: data analyst

slides.title: The Survey
slides.storyContext: Raj asks classmates: 'What is your favorite subject?' Meera organizes the answers: Math (8), Science (6), English (4), Hindi (5), Sports (7).
slides.inSimpleWords: Data is information we collect and organize.

image.alt: The Survey — Data Handling and Presentation

slides.title: What is Data?

points.label: Definition
points.text: Data is facts and figures collected through observation, measurement, or surveys.

points.label: Examples
points.text: Heights of students, favorite colors, test scores, number of books read.

slides.inSimpleWords: Data tells us about the world using numbers and facts.

slides.title: Collecting Data
slides.storyContext: Meera explains: data can come from surveys, observations, or measurements. Always ask clear questions.

points.label: Types of Data
points.text: Qualitative (colors, preferences), Quantitative (numbers, measurements).

slides.inSimpleWords: Data is facts and information collected carefully.

image.alt: Collecting Data — Data Handling and Presentation

slides.title: Survey Question Example

example.problem: Write a clear survey question to collect favorite sports from 25 classmates.
example.solution: Bad: 'Do you like sports?' Good: 'Which sport do you like best: Cricket, Football, Basketball, Badminton, or Tennis?' Clear options make data easier to collect.

slides.inSimpleWords: Good survey questions have clear choices and no confusing words.

slides.title: The Counting Begins
slides.storyContext: Raj pulls out tally marks. 'One for Math... two for Math... Meera, your turn to count Science votes!'
slides.inSimpleWords: Tallying tracks data as it comes in.

slides.title: Tally Marks System

points.label: Single Mark
points.text: One mark = one vote: |

points.label: Group of Five
points.text: Five marks in a group: ||||/

points.label: Counting
points.text: Makes it easy to count to 5, then 10, then 15...

slides.inSimpleWords: Tally marks are quick and help count to five.

slides.title: Tallying and Frequency
slides.storyContext: Raj uses tally marks to count: Math |||||| || (8 votes), Science |||| | (6 votes).

example.problem: Make a frequency table for favorite colors: Red (7), Blue (9), Green (5), Yellow (4).
example.solution:
Color | Tally | Frequency
Red | |||||| | 7
Blue | |||||||| | 9
Green | ||||| | 5
Yellow | |||| | 4

slides.inSimpleWords: Tally marks and frequency tables organize counted data.

image.alt: Tallying and Frequency — Data Handling and Presentation

slides.title: Organizing the Results
slides.storyContext: Raj and Meera sit together after the survey. Meera says, 'Now let's put this in order: first count, then table, then a picture everyone can read.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Once we collect data, we arrange it step by step.

slides.title: Frequency Table

points.label: What it is
points.text: A table listing each item and how many times it appears (its frequency).

points.label: How to use
points.text: Count tally marks for each category. Sum the tallies to get frequency.

slides.inSimpleWords: A frequency table shows what and how many.

slides.title: Building a Frequency Table

example.problem: Students were asked 'What breakfast do you eat?' Tally: Idli 9, Dosa 7, Upma 5, Paratha 4. Create a frequency table.
example.solution:
Breakfast | Tally | Frequency
Idli | ||||||||| | 9
Dosa | ||||||| | 7
Upma | ||||| | 5
Paratha | |||| | 4

slides.inSimpleWords: Write the item name, draw tallies, count the tallies for frequency.

slides.title: Time to Draw
slides.storyContext: Meera pulls out colored pencils. 'Raj, let's make a picture of our data. A chart anyone can understand at a glance!'
slides.inSimpleWords: Charts and pictures tell data stories visually.

slides.title: Pictographs and Bar Charts
slides.storyContext: Meera draws a bar chart: each bar's height shows how many votes each subject got.

points.label: Pictograph
points.text: Uses pictures to represent data; 1 picture = a fixed number of items.

points.label: Bar Chart
points.text: Uses rectangular bars to compare quantities across categories.

slides.inSimpleWords: Charts make data easy to see and compare at a glance.

image.alt: Pictographs and Bar Charts — Data Handling and Presentation

slides.title: Reading a Pictograph

example.problem: A pictograph shows favorite fruits: Apple (3 🍎), Mango (4 🥭), Banana (2 🍌). Each symbol = 2 students. How many students like mango?
example.solution: 4 symbols × 2 students per symbol = 8 students like mango.

slides.inSimpleWords: Count the pictures and multiply by the 'value per picture'.

slides.title: Making a Bar Chart
slides.storyContext: Raj draws the favorite subject bar chart: y-axis = number of votes (0-8), x-axis = subjects.

example.problem: Draw a bar chart for favorite sport: Cricket (10), Football (8), Basketball (6), Tennis (4).
example.solution: Bars rise to 10, 8, 6, 4 respectively. Cricket has the tallest bar, tennis the shortest.

slides.inSimpleWords: Height of bar = amount of data for that category.

image.alt: Making a Bar Chart — Data Handling and Presentation

slides.title: Analyzing the Data
slides.storyContext: Meera looks at their chart and asks, 'What number is in the middle? Which subject appears most often? What's the average?'
slides.inSimpleWords: Once we display data, we can find patterns and meaning.

slides.title: Mean, Median, Mode
slides.storyContext: Meera analyzes the vote numbers: Mean (average), Median (middle), Mode (most common).

points.label: Mean
points.text: Sum of all values ÷ number of values.

points.label: Median
points.text: Middle value when arranged in order.

points.label: Mode
points.text: Value that appears most often.

slides.inSimpleWords: Mean is average, median is middle, mode is most common.

image.alt: Mean, Median, Mode — Data Handling and Presentation

slides.title: Calculating Mean

example.problem: Heights of 4 students: 140 cm, 145 cm, 135 cm, 150 cm. Find mean height.

slides.inSimpleWords: Add all values, divide by how many there are.

slides.title: Finding Median

example.problem: Test scores: 78, 82, 75, 90, 88. Find the median.
example.solution: Order: 75, 78, 82, 88, 90. Middle value = 82 (3rd of 5 values).

slides.inSimpleWords: Sort from smallest to largest, pick the middle.

slides.title: Identifying Mode

example.problem: Favorite colors: Blue, Red, Blue, Green, Blue, Red, Yellow. Find the mode.
example.solution: Blue appears 3 times, Red 2 times, Green 1, Yellow 1. Mode = Blue.

slides.inSimpleWords: Count which one repeats most; that's the mode.

slides.title: Finding Mean, Median, Mode
slides.storyContext: Vote counts: 8, 6, 4, 5, 7. Find mean, median, mode.

example.problem: Scores: 8, 6, 4, 5, 7. Find mean, median, mode.
example.solution: Mean = (8+6+4+5+7)÷5 = 30÷5 = 6. Median (ordered: 4,5,6,7,8) = 6. Mode = none (all appear once).

slides.inSimpleWords: Mean uses all values, median ignores outliers, mode shows preference.

image.alt: Finding Mean, Median, Mode — Data Handling and Presentation

slides.title: The Complete Journey
slides.storyContext: Meera shows Raj a poster: question → survey → tally → frequency table → chart → analysis.
slides.inSimpleWords: Data has a journey from question to understanding.

slides.title: Data Handling Steps

points.label: Step 1
points.text: Ask a clear question.

points.label: Step 2
points.text: Collect data (survey, observe, measure).

points.label: Step 3
points.text: Tally and create frequency table.

points.label: Step 4
points.text: Draw pictograph or bar chart.

points.label: Step 5
points.text: Analyze: find mean, median, mode; look for patterns.

slides.inSimpleWords: Follow steps from question to conclusion.

slides.title: Survey and Present
slides.storyContext: Meera asks Raj to survey 20 classmates on favorite games, make a bar chart, and find mean players per game.

points.label: Challenge
points.text: Collect data → Tally → Frequency table → Bar chart → Calculate mean.

slides.inSimpleWords: Go from survey to organized chart to statistical analysis.

image.alt: Survey and Present — Data Handling and Presentation

slides.title: Compare Two Datasets

example.problem: Survey 20 students on favorite meal (breakfast or lunch). Create two frequency tables, draw bar charts, compare means.
example.solution: Count votes for each meal type. Make tables side by side. Calculate mean for each. Compare which meal has higher average preference.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use data tools to compare and draw conclusions.

slides.title: Outlier Detective

example.problem: Scores: 10, 12, 11, 9, 50. Find mean, median, mode. Which is most helpful?
example.solution: Mean = 18.4 (pulled up by 50). Median = 11 (closer to reality). Mode = none. Median works best when there's an outlier.

slides.inSimpleWords: Different statistics reveal different truths.

slides.title: Data Handling Review
slides.storyContext: Raj and Meera review the complete data journey.

points.label: Collection
points.text: Ask clear questions, record carefully.

points.label: Organization
points.text: Frequency tables, pictographs, bar charts.

points.label: Analysis
points.text: Mean (average), Median (middle), Mode (most).

slides.inSimpleWords: Data tells stories when collected and presented clearly.

image.alt: Data Handling Review — Data Handling and Presentation

subject: Science
title: Raj's Nature Hike Classification
hook: Raj explores a nature trail and learns how scientists organize all living things.

characters.name: Raj
characters.role: naturalist

characters.name: Meera
characters.role: nature guide

slides.title: Nature Trail Discovery
slides.storyContext: During a hike, Raj spots plants, insects, birds, and mammals. Meera explains these are all organisms, but they're organized into different groups.
slides.inSimpleWords: Living things come in many different types.

image.alt: Nature Trail Discovery — Diversity in the Living World

slides.title: What Makes Things Alive?
slides.storyContext: Meera shows Raj that all living things move, eat, grow, reproduce, and respond to their environment.

points.label: Characteristics
points.text: Growth, reproduction, response to environment, use of energy, homeostasis.

slides.inSimpleWords: Living things grow, move, reproduce, and respond to their world.

image.alt: What Makes Things Alive? — Diversity in the Living World

slides.title: Is It Alive? Test

example.problem: Is a virus alive? It reproduces but needs a host cell. Is a crystal alive? It grows but doesn't reproduce.
example.solution: Virus: debate between scientists. Crystal: no—doesn't eat, move, or reproduce on its own. Both fail at least one 'alive' test.

slides.inSimpleWords: Living things must grow, eat, and reproduce all by themselves.

slides.title: Sorting Living Things
slides.storyContext: Meera takes out a chart. 'Scientists have five main groups for all life on Earth. Let's see how each one lives differently.'
slides.inSimpleWords: All life on Earth fits into five big groups.

slides.title: The Five Kingdoms
slides.storyContext: Raj learns the five kingdoms: Animals (move, eat), Plants (make own food), Fungi (decompose), Protists (single-celled mostly), Bacteria (tiny, everywhere).

example.problem: Classify these as animal, plant, or fungus: dog, rice, mushroom, tree, ant.
example.solution: Dog and ant are animals. Rice and tree are plants. Mushroom is fungus.

slides.inSimpleWords: Five major kingdoms organize all life on Earth.

image.alt: Kingdom Kingdoms — Diversity in the Living World

slides.title: Kingdom Features

points.label: Animals
points.text: Eat food, move around, have many cells (dogs, insects, humans).

points.label: Plants
points.text: Make own food using sunlight, stay in place (trees, grass, flowers).

points.label: Fungi
points.text: Break down dead things (mushrooms, yeast, mold).

points.label: Protists
points.text: Mostly single-celled, simple (amoeba, algae).

points.label: Bacteria
points.text: Microscopic, everywhere (in soil, gut, water).

slides.inSimpleWords: Each kingdom has its own way of living.

slides.title: Inside the Animal Kingdom
slides.storyContext: Meera points to a bird and a butterfly. 'Notice: the bird has bones and a backbone. The butterfly doesn't. This is a big difference.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Animals split into two big groups by backbone.

slides.title: Vertebrates and Invertebrates
slides.storyContext: Raj notices the bird has bones (backbone), but the butterfly doesn't. Meera explains vertebrates have spines, invertebrates don't.

points.label: Vertebrates
points.text: Have backbone: fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, mammals.

points.label: Invertebrates
points.text: No backbone: insects, worms, crustaceans, mollusks, spiders.

slides.inSimpleWords: Vertebrates have backbones, invertebrates don't.

image.alt: Vertebrates and Invertebrates — Diversity in the Living World

slides.title: Vertebrate Groups

points.label: Fish
points.text: Live in water, have gills, cold-blooded (goldfish, sharks).

points.label: Amphibians
points.text: Live part in water, part on land (frogs, toads).

points.label: Reptiles
points.text: Dry skin, cold-blooded (snakes, lizards, crocodiles).

points.label: Birds
points.text: Have feathers, lay eggs, warm-blooded (sparrows, eagles).

points.label: Mammals
points.text: Have hair, warm-blooded, feed milk to babies (dogs, whales, humans).

slides.inSimpleWords: Vertebrates are organized by how they survive.

slides.title: Animal Classification
slides.storyContext: Raj sorts animals he sees: sparrow (bird), lizard (reptile), beetle (insect), frog (amphibian), fish (fish).

example.problem: Classify: whale, snake, octopus, cow, eagle.
example.solution: Whale and cow are mammals. Snake is reptile. Octopus is mollusk. Eagle is bird.

slides.inSimpleWords: Groups share features: birds have feathers, fish have gills, mammals feed milk.

image.alt: Animal Classification — Diversity in the Living World

slides.title: Plant Discoveries
slides.storyContext: The hikers see soft moss on a wet rock, fern fronds in the shade, and bright flowers in sunlight. 'All plants, but so different!' says Meera.
slides.inSimpleWords: Plants have a journey too: from simplest to most complex.

slides.title: Plants: Different Types
slides.storyContext: Meera points out mosses (no roots), ferns (have roots but no seeds), and flowering plants (have seeds and flowers).

points.label: Mosses
points.text: Simple plants, no roots or seeds, reproduce by spores.

points.label: Ferns
points.text: Have roots and leaves, reproduce by spores.

points.label: Seed Plants
points.text: Flowering and cone-bearing plants, reproduce by seeds.

slides.inSimpleWords: Plants get more complex: mosses → ferns → seed plants.

image.alt: Plants: Different Types — Diversity in the Living World

slides.title: Moss and Fern Details

points.label: Moss
points.text: Soft, spongy, grows on damp places, no real roots.

points.label: Fern
points.text: Has thin roots, green leaflets, likes shade and moisture.

slides.inSimpleWords: Mosses are simple; ferns are in the middle.

slides.title: Seed Plants

points.label: Flowering Plants
points.text: Have flowers, colorful petals, fruit with seeds (roses, tomatoes).

points.label: Cone-bearing Plants
points.text: Have cones with seeds, usually evergreen (pine, spruce).

slides.inSimpleWords: Most plants we see have flowers or cones.

slides.title: Finding Plant Types
slides.storyContext: Raj identifies moss on a rock, fern in shade, and flowers in sunlight on the trail.

example.problem: You find three plants: one very simple on wet rock, one with leaves but no flowers, one with bright flowers. Classify each.
example.solution: Rock plant is moss. Leafy plant is fern. Flowering plant is a seed plant (flowering plant).

slides.inSimpleWords: Observe roots, seeds, and leaves to identify plant types.

image.alt: Finding Plant Types — Diversity in the Living World

slides.title: The Hidden World
slides.storyContext: 'Look at this soil,' says Meera. 'Fungi, bacteria, tiny animals—billions of living things we can't see. All part of Earth's diversity.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Life exists at every scale, seen and unseen.

slides.title: Fungi and Microorganisms

points.label: Fungi
points.text: Break down dead plants and animals, help soil, many are visible (mushrooms, yeast).

points.label: Bacteria
points.text: Single-celled, everywhere, some help (yogurt, compost) and some cause disease.

points.label: Protists
points.text: Mostly single-celled, move in water, include algae that make oxygen.

slides.inSimpleWords: Fungi and bacteria are nature's recyclers.

slides.title: Microorganisms Around Us

example.problem: Name 3 helpful bacteria or fungi and 3 harmful ones.
example.solution: Helpful: yogurt bacteria, compost fungi, algae. Harmful: skin fungus, disease bacteria, food-spoiling fungi.

slides.inSimpleWords: Microbes are everywhere—some help us, some harm us.

slides.title: Connecting All Life
slides.storyContext: 'Every kingdom depends on the others,' explains Meera. 'Plants make oxygen, animals spread seeds, fungi decompose everything. It's all connected.'
slides.inSimpleWords: All five kingdoms work together in nature.

slides.title: How Nature Groups Organisms
slides.storyContext: Meera draws a tree: Kingdom splits into groups, groups split into more specific groups. 'It's like a family tree of all life,' she says.
slides.inSimpleWords: Scientists organize life by shared traits.

slides.title: Classification Hierarchy

points.label: Kingdom
points.text: Broadest group (Animals, Plants, Fungi, Protists, Bacteria).

points.label: Phylum
points.text: Major division within kingdom (Chordata for animals with backbone).

points.label: Class
points.text: Further grouping (Mammals, Birds, Reptiles within Chordata).

slides.inSimpleWords: Classification goes from broad to narrow.

slides.title: Classify Your Neighborhood
slides.storyContext: Meera challenges Raj to list 10 organisms he sees at home and classify each by kingdom and type.

points.label: Challenge
points.text: Note at least one animal, one plant, and one microorganism (like fungus bread mold).

slides.inSimpleWords: Look around and classify living things by their features.

image.alt: Classify Your Neighborhood — Diversity in the Living World

slides.title: Sort a Food Web

example.problem: In a garden: plants, grasshoppers, birds, fungus on dead leaves. Classify each into kingdom and type.
example.solution: Plants are in Kingdom Plantae. Grasshopper and bird are Kingdom Animalia (insect and bird). Fungus is Kingdom Fungi.

slides.inSimpleWords: Even food chains show the five kingdoms.

slides.title: Backbone vs. No Backbone

example.problem: List 5 vertebrates you know and 5 invertebrates. Draw a line down the middle.
example.solution: Vertebrates: dog, sparrow, fish, human, snake. Invertebrates: ant, worm, butterfly, crab, octopus.

slides.inSimpleWords: Practice spotting the backbone difference.

slides.title: Diversity Review
slides.storyContext: Raj and Meera finish the hike, appreciating Earth's incredible variety of life.

points.label: Kingdoms
points.text: Animals, Plants, Fungi, Protists, Bacteria.

points.label: Animals
points.text: Vertebrates (backbone) or Invertebrates (no backbone).

points.label: Plants
points.text: Mosses, Ferns, or Seed Plants (simple to complex).

slides.inSimpleWords: Life's diversity is organized by shared features.

image.alt: Diversity Review — Diversity in the Living World

subject: Science
title: Meera's Magnetic Adventure
hook: Meera discovers invisible forces when magnets attract and repel around her home.

characters.name: Meera
characters.role: magnet explorer

characters.name: Raj
characters.role: assistant

slides.title: Magnetic Discovery
slides.storyContext: Meera picks up iron nails with a magnet. Raj asks, 'Why do they stick?' Meera explains that magnets have invisible pulling power.
slides.inSimpleWords: Magnets are objects with invisible pulling and pushing forces.

image.alt: Magnetic Discovery — Exploring Magnets

slides.title: What is a Magnet?
slides.storyContext: Meera shows different magnets: bar magnet, horseshoe magnet, electromagnet. They all attract iron and steel.

points.label: Magnet
points.text: Object with magnetic field; attracts iron and steel; has poles (north and south).

slides.inSimpleWords: A magnet attracts certain metals without touching them.

image.alt: What is a Magnet? — Exploring Magnets

slides.title: Types of Magnets

points.label: Bar Magnet
points.text: Rectangle shape, strong at ends (poles), used in experiments.

points.label: Horseshoe Magnet
points.text: Curved, poles at ends, stronger than bar magnet for same size.

points.label: Electromagnet
points.text: Coil of wire with electricity, can be switched on/off, used in doorbells and motors.

slides.inSimpleWords: Different magnet shapes have different strengths.

slides.title: Testing the Kitchen
slides.storyContext: Raj brings a magnet through the kitchen. 'Metal spoon—yes! Plastic cup—no! Aluminum foil—no! This is interesting!'
slides.inSimpleWords: Not all metal things are magnetic.

slides.title: Magnetic and Non-Magnetic
slides.storyContext: Meera tests objects: iron (attracted), aluminum foil (not attracted), steel (attracted), plastic (not attracted).

example.problem: Test these with a magnet: nail, rubber, coin, spoon, plastic bag.
example.solution: Nail and spoon attract (if metal). Rubber, coin, plastic bag don't attract.

slides.inSimpleWords: Iron, steel, and nickel are magnetic; most others are not.

image.alt: Magnetic and Non-Magnetic — Exploring Magnets

slides.title: What Can Be Magnetized?

points.label: Iron
points.text: Strongly attracted to magnets; can become a magnet itself.

points.label: Steel
points.text: Contains iron, also attracts to magnets.

points.label: Nickel and Cobalt
points.text: Weakly attracted to magnets.

points.label: Aluminum, Copper, Gold
points.text: Not attracted to ordinary magnets.

slides.inSimpleWords: Only certain metals respond to magnets.

slides.title: The Invisible Battle
slides.storyContext: Meera holds two bar magnets. 'Feel this—they push against each other! And now... they pull! Raj, swap one magnet's direction—now they push again!'
slides.inSimpleWords: Magnets can pull together or push apart.

slides.title: Magnetic Poles
slides.storyContext: Meera labels a bar magnet: North pole (N) and South pole (S). She notices they attract but opposite poles repel each other.

points.label: Poles
points.text: Every magnet has North and South poles. Opposite poles attract, like poles repel.

slides.inSimpleWords: N and S poles attract each other. N-N or S-S repel.

image.alt: Magnetic Poles — Exploring Magnets

slides.title: Attraction and Repulsion
slides.storyContext: Raj holds two bar magnets: N-S together (pull), N-N together (push). Meera explains the rule.

example.problem: Magnet A (N-S) and Magnet B (N-S). If A's north faces B's south, do they attract or repel?
example.solution: Opposite poles (N-S) attract each other.

slides.inSimpleWords: Opposite poles attract, same poles push away.

image.alt: Attraction and Repulsion — Exploring Magnets

slides.title: Earth Compass
slides.storyContext: Meera pulls out a compass and spins it. 'No matter which way I turn it, the needle always points north. Why?'
slides.inSimpleWords: Earth itself is a giant magnet.

slides.title: Earth's Magnetism

points.label: Earth is a Magnet
points.text: Liquid iron core creates Earth's magnetic field.

points.label: Compass
points.text: Needle aligns with Earth's field, north needle points to magnetic north.

points.label: Aurora
points.text: Colorful lights at poles caused by Earth's magnetic field.

slides.inSimpleWords: Earth itself is a giant magnet.

slides.title: The Pattern in Iron Filings
slides.storyContext: Meera spreads iron filings on paper above a magnet. 'Look, Raj—they line up! This shows the invisible shape of the magnet's power.'
slides.inSimpleWords: We can see the magnetic field with iron filings.

slides.title: Magnetic Field
slides.storyContext: Meera sprinkles iron filings around a magnet. The filings arrange in a pattern, showing the invisible magnetic field.

points.label: Magnetic Field
points.text: Invisible region around a magnet where magnetic force acts.

slides.inSimpleWords: Magnetic field is the invisible area where magnet's force works.

image.alt: Magnetic Field — Exploring Magnets

slides.title: Field Lines and Patterns

points.label: Pattern Shape
points.text: Field lines curve from north to south pole outside magnet, south to north inside.

points.label: Field Strength
points.text: Stronger at poles, weaker farther away.

slides.inSimpleWords: Field lines show how the magnet's force spreads.

slides.title: Observing Magnetic Fields
slides.storyContext: Iron filings create patterns around the magnet showing field lines radiating from poles.

example.problem: A magnet attracts a nail from 5 cm away. Is the nail in the magnetic field?
example.solution: Yes, the nail feels attraction from 5 cm away, so it's in the magnetic field region.

slides.inSimpleWords: If a magnet pulls something without touching, it's in the magnetic field.

image.alt: Observing Magnetic Fields — Exploring Magnets

slides.title: Testing Thickness
slides.storyContext: Meera puts paper, then glass, then water between a magnet and nail. 'Raj, the nail still moves! Does the magnet's force go through everything?'
slides.inSimpleWords: Magnetic force is special—it travels through barriers.

slides.title: Magnetic Force Through Materials

points.label: Through Paper
points.text: Magnetic force passes through easily, barely weakens.

points.label: Through Glass
points.text: Force passes through, slight weakening.

points.label: Through Water
points.text: Force passes through, weakens a little.

points.label: Through Plastic
points.text: Force passes through unchanged.

points.label: Through Iron
points.text: Force cannot pass; iron blocks it.

slides.inSimpleWords: Most materials let magnetic force through.

slides.title: Force Through Barriers

example.problem: You have a magnet and nail separated by 2 cm of paper. Will the nail attract to the magnet?
example.solution: Yes, magnetic force passes through paper almost unchanged. The nail will still move toward the magnet.

slides.inSimpleWords: Magnetic force is powerful enough to penetrate most barriers.

slides.title: Testing Different Materials

example.problem: Test these 5 materials with a magnet: iron nail, copper coin, aluminum foil, rubber, wooden pencil. Which attract?
example.solution: Only the iron nail attracts. Copper, aluminum, rubber, and wood do not attract to a magnet.

slides.inSimpleWords: Always test to discover what is magnetic.

slides.title: Magnets in Action
slides.storyContext: 'Magnets aren't just toys,' says Meera. 'Look around: doorbells use electromagnets, motors use them, even scrapyards use them to lift cars!'
slides.inSimpleWords: Magnets power everyday devices.

slides.title: Uses of Magnets

points.label: Electromagnets
points.text: Doorbells, motors, switches, medical scanners (MRI).

points.label: Permanent Magnets
points.text: Compasses, fridge magnets, speakers, hard drives.

points.label: Industrial
points.text: Scrapyards lift metal, mining, metal separation.

slides.inSimpleWords: Magnets are essential in technology and industry.

slides.title: Magnet Experiments
slides.storyContext: Meera challenges Raj to predict: will a magnet work through paper? Glass? Water? Test and explain.

points.label: Challenge
points.text: Magnetic force passes through paper and glass but weakens. Water also allows force to pass.

slides.inSimpleWords: Magnetic fields pass through many materials.

image.alt: Magnet Experiments — Exploring Magnets

slides.title: Design a Magnet Game

example.problem: Design a game using two magnets to move metal objects without touching them. Describe the rules.
example.solution: Place objects on paper above/below one magnet. Use another magnet to repel and attract them. Score points for moving to targets.

slides.inSimpleWords: Invisible forces can do real work.

slides.title: Predict Pole Interactions

example.problem: Three unlabeled magnets. Use a compass to find which pole is north on each, then predict attraction/repulsion.
example.solution: Compass needle points to south pole of magnet (north-seeking). Opposite poles attract, same repel.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use tools to discover hidden properties.

slides.title: Magnets Review
slides.storyContext: Meera and Raj explore everyday magnets: in compasses, door latches, magnetic stickers.

points.label: Basics
points.text: Magnets attract iron/steel via invisible poles (N and S).

points.label: Rules
points.text: Opposite poles attract, like poles repel, field passes through materials.

points.label: Uses
points.text: Compasses, electromagnets, motors, toys, separation tools.

slides.inSimpleWords: Magnets are forces that work through invisible fields.

image.alt: Magnets Review — Exploring Magnets

subject: Science
title: Raj's Running Track Measurements
hook: Raj measures distances and times his runs, learning to quantify motion.

characters.name: Raj
characters.role: athlete

characters.name: Meera
characters.role: scientist

slides.title: Raj's Running Track Measurements
slides.storyContext: Raj and Meera explore how to measure distance and motion at their local sports track.

slides.title: Track Day
slides.storyContext: Raj wants to know how far he runs and how fast. Meera brings measuring tape and stopwatch.
slides.inSimpleWords: Length tells us distance, time tells us how fast.

image.alt: Track Day — Measurement of Length and Motion

slides.title: What is Measurement?
slides.storyContext: Meera explains: measurement means comparing something to a standard unit. Length is how far, width is how broad.

points.label: Measurement
points.text: Comparing an object to a standard unit (like a meter) to find its size or distance.

points.label: Why We Measure
points.text: To compare, track progress, and understand the physical world accurately.

slides.inSimpleWords: Measurement compares something to a known standard unit.

slides.title: Standard Units of Length
slides.storyContext: Meera explains: centimeter (cm), meter (m), kilometer (km). The meter is the standard unit.

points.label: Metric Units
points.text: mm (millimeter), cm (centimeter), m (meter), km (kilometer). 1 m = 100 cm.

slides.inSimpleWords: Meter is the main unit; 100 cm = 1 meter.

image.alt: Standard Units of Length — Measurement of Length and Motion

slides.title: Measuring Length
slides.storyContext: Raj measures the track: 100 meters long. Using a measuring tape, he records: 100.0 m.

example.problem: A track is 100 meters. Express in centimeters and kilometers.
example.solution: 100 m = 10,000 cm (multiply by 100). 100 m = 0.1 km (divide by 1,000).

slides.inSimpleWords: Convert between units: multiply or divide by 10s.

image.alt: Measuring Length — Measurement of Length and Motion

slides.title: Measuring Tools Around Us
slides.storyContext: Raj finds a meter scale, measuring tape, ruler, and even his own arm span. Each tool measures distance.

points.label: Ruler
points.text: Short distances, 15–30 cm long.

points.label: Measuring Tape
points.text: Longer distances up to 50 m, flexible.

points.label: Meter Scale
points.text: Exactly 1 meter, rigid, precise.

slides.inSimpleWords: Different tools measure different lengths: rulers for small, tapes for long.

slides.title: Estimating vs Measuring
slides.storyContext: Meera asks Raj: guess the distance across the field first, then measure it. How close was your estimate?

points.label: Challenge
points.text: Develop estimation skills: pacing (steps), arm span, reference objects. Compare to measured values.

slides.inSimpleWords: Estimation uses body reference (arm, steps); measurement uses tools for accuracy.

slides.title: Time Measurement
slides.storyContext: Meera uses a stopwatch to time Raj's run. She records seconds, minutes.

points.label: Units
points.text: Second (s), minute (min), hour (h). 1 min = 60 s, 1 hour = 60 min.

slides.inSimpleWords: Second is the main unit; 60 seconds = 1 minute.

image.alt: Time Measurement — Measurement of Length and Motion

slides.title: Time and Speed Connection
slides.storyContext: Meera explains: speed links distance and time. The same distance takes different times at different speeds.

points.label: Slow Motion
points.text: Long distance, long time = slow speed (e.g., walk).

points.label: Fast Motion
points.text: Long distance, short time = fast speed (e.g., sprint).

slides.inSimpleWords: Faster motion covers distance in less time.

slides.title: Calculating Speed
slides.storyContext: Raj runs 100 meters in 20 seconds. Meera calculates his speed: 100÷20 = 5 meters per second.

example.problem: Raj runs 100 m in 20 s. What is his speed?
example.solution: Speed = distance ÷ time = 100 m ÷ 20 s = 5 m/s (meters per second).

slides.inSimpleWords: Speed = distance traveled ÷ time taken.

image.alt: Calculating Speed — Measurement of Length and Motion

slides.title: Motion Concepts
slides.storyContext: Meera explains: motion is change in position. Speed is how fast, velocity includes direction.

points.label: Speed
points.text: How fast something moves: distance ÷ time.

points.label: Velocity
points.text: Speed with direction: '5 m/s north'.

points.label: Acceleration
points.text: Change in speed or direction: speeding up, slowing down.

slides.inSimpleWords: Speed shows how fast, velocity includes direction.

image.alt: Motion Concepts — Measurement of Length and Motion

slides.title: Distance vs Displacement
slides.storyContext: Raj runs around the track and returns to start: distance = 400 m (full lap), displacement = 0 (no net position change).

points.label: Distance
points.text: Total path traveled, always positive.

points.label: Displacement
points.text: Straight-line change in position, can be zero.

slides.inSimpleWords: Distance is how much you travel, displacement is how far from start.

slides.title: Real Motion Scenarios
slides.storyContext: Raj experiments: walk at constant speed (slow), jog (medium), sprint (fast), then suddenly stop.

example.problem: Raj walks 30 m in 10 s, then runs 50 m in 10 s. Which is faster?
example.solution: Walk: 30÷10 = 3 m/s. Run: 50÷10 = 5 m/s. Running is faster.

slides.inSimpleWords: Faster motion covers more distance in same time.

image.alt: Real Motion Scenarios — Measurement of Length and Motion

slides.title: Average Speed Over a Journey
slides.storyContext: Meera tracks Raj's jog: 1 km in 5 minutes. Average speed = 1000 m ÷ 300 s = 3.3 m/s.

points.label: Average Speed
points.text: Total distance ÷ total time. Smooths out ups and downs.

slides.inSimpleWords: Average speed = total distance ÷ total time taken.

slides.title: Speed in Different Units
slides.storyContext: A car travels 60 km in 1 hour (60 km/h). Convert to m/s: 60,000 m ÷ 3,600 s = 16.7 m/s.

example.problem: A car travels at 60 km/h. Express in m/s.
example.solution: 60 km/h = 60,000 m ÷ 3,600 s = 16.7 m/s. (Divide km/h by 3.6 for m/s.)

slides.inSimpleWords: Convert between km/h and m/s by multiplying/dividing by 3.6.

slides.title: Uniform vs Non-Uniform Motion
slides.storyContext: Meera explains: Raj's constant jog = uniform (same speed every second). His sprint start = non-uniform (speed changes).

points.label: Uniform Motion
points.text: Constant speed, equal distances in equal time intervals.

points.label: Non-Uniform Motion
points.text: Speed changes; different distances in equal time intervals.

slides.inSimpleWords: Uniform = same speed always. Non-uniform = speed keeps changing.

slides.title: Measuring Stopwatch Accuracy
slides.storyContext: Raj and Meera test stopwatch reaction time: start on '3, 2, 1, go!' vs. by sight. Who has faster reaction?

points.label: Challenge
points.text: Human reaction time adds 0.1–0.3 seconds error. Design an experiment to measure it.

slides.inSimpleWords: Reaction time is a source of measurement error; try to minimize it.

slides.title: Position-Time Graphs
slides.storyContext: Meera plots Raj's position vs time: straight line = constant speed, steep = fast, flat = stopped.

points.label: Slope Meaning
points.text: Steeper slope = faster speed. Horizontal line = stationary.

slides.inSimpleWords: On a graph, steeper lines mean faster motion.

slides.title: Motion Analysis
slides.storyContext: Meera challenges Raj to measure his friend's 200 m dash time and calculate speed.

points.label: Challenge
points.text: If 200 m in 40 s, then speed = 200÷40 = 5 m/s.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use stopwatch and measuring tape to find real speeds.

image.alt: Motion Analysis — Measurement of Length and Motion

slides.title: Obstacles and Errors in Measuring
slides.storyContext: Raj notices: the track is not perfectly straight, wind affects timing, human reaction time adds error to stopwatch.

points.label: Systematic Errors
points.text: Measuring tape stretches, track curves, instrument calibration.

points.label: Human Errors
points.text: Reaction time on stopwatch, not reading scale correctly.

slides.inSimpleWords: Real measurements have small errors; try to minimize them.

slides.title: Acceleration Calculations
slides.storyContext: Raj starts at rest and reaches 5 m/s after 2 seconds. Acceleration = (5 − 0) ÷ 2 = 2.5 m/s².

example.problem: Raj accelerates from rest to 10 m/s in 4 seconds. Find acceleration.
example.solution: Acceleration = (10 − 0) ÷ 4 = 2.5 m/s². (Velocity change ÷ time.)

slides.inSimpleWords: Acceleration = change in speed ÷ time taken.

slides.title: Relative Motion
